verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You feel hurt after being skipped for promotion again, and you are starting to think they might be right about you. Bhartrihari cries out to Hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart while trying to please the wicked. Today, this speaks to the weight of performing for approval that still leaves you unseen. You do not have to keep dancing on that empty stage; you can let your hands fall.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to his own hope from the section called Censure of Craving. He has spent his life digging for treasure, flattering kings, and enduring humiliation to win favour. Now he lists the taunts he swallowed, the tears he held back, and the forced smiles he wore before people numbed by wealth. He asks hope how much longer it will make him dance in this servile way. You are carrying the weight of performing for approval that still leaves you unseen. Bhartrihari names the cost of swallowing insults to keep a chance alive.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You wonder if you are not leadership material while your manager gives visible projects to others. Manu tells Vishnu that, finding the wishing tree, he still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power. Your doubt rises because you feel too small for what you want, yet the verse points to a generosity that outruns your uncertainty. You can name the project you want, trusting that the one offering it is larger than your fear.
meaning: Manu speaks to Vishnu after years of austerity. The Lord offers him any boon. Manu hesitates, comparing himself to a poor man who finds a wishing tree yet shrinks from asking for much, not knowing its power. He finally asks for a son like God himself. The verse proposes that it is not too late to turn toward what matters, but it takes courage to ask for it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: Karmaṇy evādhikāras te: your right is to the action. Fear of failure is a fear about the fruit, which was never given to you to control. Krishna also closes the escape route: don't let this make you stop acting. Care, prepare and aim well, then put the outcome down.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is afraid to fight and wonders whether action is worth it. Krishna tells him to do his work fully. He says the right to act belongs to you, but the results do not. Do not make the outcome your motive, and do not use that as a reason to sit still. Your boss puts your mistakes on display in front of everyone. That makes you feel like you are useless. The verse says the work is yours, but the result is not yours to hold.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: Since the breakup, weekends feel like they belong only to you, and the friends around you were really his. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet some ache is so private that no one else can truly share it. Your heart alone knows the love you miss. You might let that private knowing sit with you this weekend, without trying to explain it to anyone.
meaning: Ram speaks these words to Sita through Hanuman. Sita is captive and near despair. Hanuman has told her Ram's story and dropped Ram's ring. Ram says that telling grief lightens it a little. But he asks whom he can tell, because no one else knows this pain. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: After your divorce, you moved to a new city to start fresh and you do not know a single person there. Krishna tells Arjuna, "See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me." When the world feels empty of familiar faces, this verse names a bond that distance cannot break: the divine never loses sight of you, and you are never out of its sight.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has asked how a person can keep a steady mind when the senses pull in every direction. Krishna answers that the one who sees him in all beings and all beings in him will never be lost to him, nor he to the one. It proposes a way of seeing that settles the mind through moderation and gentle return. You are learning to live in a place where no face is known yet. This verse names a bond that distance cannot break, even when the city holds no one you recognize.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You did not realise how much of your life was him, and now that he is abroad, the silence can feel vast. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet asks whom he can tell, since no one else knows this ache. Your heart alone holds the truth of what you miss, and naming that private weight is a real step you can take today.
meaning: Ram sends this message to Sita through Hanuman. Sita sits captive in the grove, threatened by Ravana, and has nearly lost hope. Hanuman has just dropped Ram's ring from a tree and told her Ram's whole story. Sita has said that Ram alone has been her ship across a sea of separation. Ram replies that speaking of pain lightens it a little. Yet he asks whom he can tell, since no one else knows this ache. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them. The silence where his voice used to be is not small. It holds a shape you only just noticed.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sitting by his window, feels mocked by this cycle. You have been firefighting so long that there is nothing left in the tank. This verse names that exact loop: the same day, again and again, until even a thoughtful mind feels the repetition is absurd. It does not ask you to push harder or to find a new meaning today; it simply holds the mirror to the cycle you are in.
meaning: Bali, a king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and looks out at his life. He sees that day follows night, and the same tasks return in an endless chain. He speaks these words to himself, feeling that a thinking person is mocked by such repetition. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the way forward is not more of the same work but mastering the mind that runs it. You have been firefighting every day for so long that your reserves are gone. This verse names the loop you are caught in without asking you to justify it or escape it today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go; they do not last, so bear them patiently. You feel the weight of work pressure that never eases, and a tiredness so deep that even the weekend keeps you in bed. This verse speaks to that rhythm: the strain touches you and moves on, and you can meet it without panic until it passes.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after the grief of battle has settled on him. Arjuna fears that if the self never dies, then every hurt should last forever. Krishna answers that the senses meet the world and feelings like heat and cold, pleasure and pain arise. They begin and they end. They do not stay. So Arjuna is asked to bear them without being swept away by either joy or grief. Your work pressure and this bone tiredness follow the same rhythm. They touch you and then they move on, even when it does not feel that way.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your mind is spinning about whether the launch will work, and you cannot sleep because of it. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. This verse names exactly that struggle, showing that a mind racing at night is not a personal failure but a real force. When you lie awake replaying what might go wrong, you are in the company of the Gita's own hero.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi who treats joy and pain as equal. Arjuna objects that such steadiness is impossible because the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna answers that practice and letting go can train it. Your mind racing about the launch is not a flaw. It is the force Arjuna names, and it is real.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel less than colleagues with MBAs because you rely only on experience. Manu says that even before the wishing tree, a poor man hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, and doubt rises in his heart. Today, your experience is real, yet you may hold back from asking for what you want because you feel too small for it. You can name what you truly want anyway, trusting that the one before you is generous.
meaning: King Manu, after years of austerity, stands before Lord Vishnu who offers him any boon. Manu hesitates to ask for what he truly desires. He compares himself to a poor man who finds a wish-fulfilling tree yet still shrinks from asking for much, not knowing the tree's power. In plain words, he says doubt rises in his heart because he feels too small to claim what is before him. Your experience carries weight that no degree can erase, yet you may shrink from asking for what you want because you feel too small beside those with MBAs.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when you keep dwelling on something, attachment is born, and from that comes desire, which blocked turns into anger. You lose your temper with your child over homework every evening and then hate yourself afterward. The verse suggests the fire may have been building earlier, in what you kept turning over in your mind, rather than only in the moment of snapping.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has just asked what a person of steady wisdom looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna answers by tracing a chain inside the mind. When a person keeps dwelling on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire. When that desire meets an obstacle and cannot reach its aim, it turns into anger. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding where attention rests, because anger begins with what a person keeps turning over before the flare. The evening snapping at your child may be the final link in a chain that started earlier, in moments when your mind kept returning to what you wanted.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You feel angry when the teenager slams doors and you yell, and then you both feel awful every week. The Yoga Vasishtha describes a mind carried along on endless waves of tasks, fainting in a net of reckonings: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Today, that same loop may be running behind your anger, not because you failed, but because the mind never gets a moment's rest. Notice one small pause between the slam and your voice, and let the depths stop dancing for just a breath.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa, two men who grew up together in a forest hermitage and later spent years apart in hard austerities. When they meet again as old men, Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found peace. Bhasa answers that he has not. He says the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks and never rests. It keeps tallying what it has done, what it is doing, and what it must still do. Caught in this net of reckonings, the bird of the mind faints. Your anger with your teenager may be riding on a loop that has nothing to do with this week alone. The mind is simply tallying tasks and never finding a place to land.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You are furious at your lead for dumping work on you, and after snapping in standup you now feel like the problem. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born; from attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. The fire may have been building while you kept turning the unfair load over in your mind. Today, the standup moment is already passed, but the dwelling that fed it remains right there, waiting.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has just asked what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna answers by tracing how the mind moves. He says that when a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and when desire is blocked, it turns into anger. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding where attention rests, because anger begins with what a person keeps turning over in the mind. The snap in standup was not the first move. The load your lead dumped on you had been turning in your mind long before the meeting started.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are waiting for emergency leave while your dad is in hospice in Delhi. Krishna, far from home, tells his mother that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name, and he has missed his morning breakfast and evening warm milk. In your waiting, the ordinary tenderness of home—being known by a home name, being fed—is what is actually missing. That absence is real, and it is shared.
meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He is far from home in Mathura after killing. He tells her to stay well and that he and his brother will return in four or five days. He adds that since the day he left, no one has called him Kanhaiya. He has not had morning breakfast or evening warm milk. The verse proposes that missing home is love. It shows that love in separation runs both ways, because Krishna, now a prince, longs for the ordinary tenderness of home.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are watching your mother slowly leave in her final stage. Krishna, far from home, tells his mother Yashoda that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name, and he has missed his morning breakfast and evening warm milk. In your distance, this voice names the small tendernesses you miss: not grand gestures, but the sound of home and being fed. Let those ordinary details be what remains real today.
meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He tells her to stay well and that the brothers will visit in a few days. He adds that since he left home, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya, and he has gone without his morning breakfast and evening warm milk. The verse shows that missing home is love, and that this love runs both ways. You are watching your mother fade, and this voice names the small tendernesses that vanish with distance, not grand gestures but the sound of home and being fed.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You miss the ordinary tenderness of home. Krishna tells his mother that since he left, no one calls him by his pet name, and he has not had his mother's morning breakfast or evening warm milk. Your guilt carries a similar ache: the distance means you are not there to share her ordinary moments, and the weight of that absence keeps returning.
meaning: Krishna sends a message to his foster mother Yashoda through. He is far from home in Mathura after killing. He tells her to stay well and that the brothers will come in four or five days. He adds that since the day he left, no one has called him Kanhaiya. He has not eaten his morning breakfast, nor had warm milk in the evening. Your guilt holds the same ache. You are not there to share her ordinary moments, and the weight of that absence keeps returning.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He is far away in Mathura after killing. He tells her they will visit in a few days. He adds that since he left, no one has called him Kanhaiya. He has missed his morning breakfast and his evening warm milk. The verse shows that missing home is love. The longing runs both ways. The prince misses the ordinary tenderness of a pet name and a mother's food.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against his own will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger. This anger clouds wisdom like smoke over fire. The verse proposes that a person can see this pattern clearly and then master it. You are asking why your temper took over when your grandmother asked her question again. The verse shows that the force you felt came from inside, not from her. Seeing that clearly is the first step toward understanding it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: The anger that flared and cost you the partnership did not appear from nowhere. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person keeps dwelling on something, attachment is born, and from that attachment comes desire, which blocked turns into anger. You do not have to carry the guilt as proof that you are the problem; you can simply notice where the mind kept returning before the snap, and let that observation be enough for now.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna asks what a person of steady wisdom looks like in speech, sitting and walking. Krishna traces the inner path from attention to ruin. He says that when a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire, when it is blocked, anger arises. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding where the mind rests, because anger starts with what a person keeps turning over. The partnership ended after words spoken in rage, and now guilt remains. This verse shows that the anger had a beginning upstream, in what your mind kept returning to before the snap.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Anger clouds judgement, clouded judgement loses memory, lost memory wrecks reason, and then you fall.
verse_text.translation: From anger comes delusion; from delusion, confusion of memory; from confusion of memory, the ruin of understanding; and with understanding ruined, a person is lost.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that anger brings delusion, then memory slips, then understanding is ruined, and you fall. This is the Gita's view of how a surge can overtake the mind you rely on to run your own thing. The partnership you lost came after the part of you that knew better had already stepped out of the room.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: It's desire, which turns into anger when blocked. Never satisfied, it is the real enemy here.
verse_text.translation: The Blessed Lord said: It is desire, it is anger, born of the quality of passion; all-devouring and greatly harmful. Know this to be the enemy here.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that desire, which becomes anger when blocked, is the real enemy here. It is never satisfied and devours everything. This points to the restless craving behind your flash of rage, giving you a clear place to stand rather than leaving you caught in the aftermath.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Unshaken in sorrow, not craving in joy, free of clinging, fear and anger: that is a steady mind.
verse_text.translation: One whose mind is not shaken by sorrow, who has no craving for pleasures, and who is free from attachment, fear and anger, is called a sage of steady mind.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a steady mind is unshaken in sorrow, not craving in joy, and free of clinging, fear and anger. You are carrying the guilt that stays after the anger flares, yet this describes a mind that still feels everything without letting sorrow or rage drive the wheel. Let that steadiness be the ground you stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Whoever can ride out the surge of desire and anger, here and now, is steady and happy.
verse_text.translation: One who is able, here in this life, before leaving the body, to withstand the surge born of desire and anger, is disciplined; he is a happy person.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever withstands the surge of desire and anger here and now is steady and happy. The surge rises and falls on its own; your only part is to wait it out before you act. You could try placing your feet flat on the floor the next time heat rushes up, and simply breathe until it passes.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse_text.line: Speak words that don't wound, that are true, kind and helpful. That is discipline of speech.
verse_text.translation: Speech that causes no distress, that is truthful, pleasant and beneficial, and the regular study of sacred texts: this is called austerity of speech.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to use speech that is true, kind, helpful and never wounds. After the surge passes, you could try filtering your next words through those four marks before they reach your partner. This does not erase what was said, but it gives your next exchange a shape that does not add fresh harm.

story.title: Vishvamitra's vow
story.summary: Vishvamitra had given up a kingdom to become a sage, and had already started his effort over more than once. Then, tested again, he lost his temper and cursed the apsara Rambha, and with that curse the power of his long austerity was spent. This time he made a vow: he would not give way to anger, or even speak. He kept a long silence. Obstacles came again and shook him, but anger couldn't get in. In the end he reached his goal, and Vasishtha, the rival he had once fought, embraced him as a friend.
story.lesson: Relapses happen. A clear vow and steady practice can loosen anger's grip.

days.reading: Vishvamitra lost his temper and spent his spiritual power, yet he began again with a clear vow to stay silent and steady. You too have known a fast flare that cost you something real. His story shows that a deliberate vow can loosen anger’s grip, even after a relapse.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You feel dropped out and without direction, as if nothing is worth the effort. Young Rama asks, what is a kingdom or pleasure to me, who am I, and what is all this for? This verse meets your emptiness as the start of a real inquiry rather than a dead end, opening the question of what truly matters to you.
meaning: Young Rama returns from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask him why he seems so low. Rama answers with a string of questions. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him. He asks who he really is and what all this is for. He says if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this naming of emptiness as the first honest step of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your sense that nothing is worth the effort names a real emptiness. It can open a question about what matters rather than closing the door on everything.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

meaning: Young Rama speaks in his father's court. He has just returned from travels. The sages ask why he seems so low. Rama answers that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship is to him, and what pleasures mean. He asks who he is, and what all this is for. He suggests that if the world is unreal, let it be unreal. He wonders whose it is, and what anyone has truly gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as despair to be fixed. Your sense that nothing matters after so much effort is a real place to stand. It is not a failure. It is the question that opens the door to seeing what is actually there.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You have spent 15 years in 12-hour days building your business, and now the work feels like nothing but exhaustion. Bali says, "Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery." That same loop of days can make the life you built feel hollow today. The verse simply names the weariness of repeating the same tasks without an ending aim, leaving you with the quiet fact of that endless chain.
meaning: The demon king Bali speaks these words to himself while sitting by his window after ruling the three worlds for ages. He notices that his days and nights run together in the same endless round of duties. He tells himself that to a thinking person this repetition feels like a mockery. After fifteen years of long days you now meet the same loop with a hollow feeling. The verse names that weariness without calling your work worthless.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse_text.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: Your mind keeps landing on tasks like a bird on food, then letting them go like a bored child's toy. Rama names this restless habit honestly, without calling it a flaw. When you sit down to study after work, this same swooping and dropping can show up again. You might notice the pattern simply as it is, and let your attention rest on the book in front of you.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha. He has grown withdrawn, and they ask him why. He answers with a lament about the world, and in it he describes the mind. The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. He is naming the restless habit honestly. He is not yet offering the answer. You feel stuck because your attention keeps landing on the screen and then leaving the book. Rama names this swooping and dropping without calling it a flaw in you.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You have a firm resolve for your GATE preparation, yet starting each day consumes half your time. Savitri tells her worried father-in-law that she began this vow with determination, and that same determination will carry her to the end. Let that same steady resolve be what pulls you through the morning, carrying your study to its close.
meaning: Savitri speaks to her blind father-in-law Dyumatsena after she begins a harsh three-night vow. She knows her husband Satyavan will die in three days. Dyumatsena is distressed by the severity of her fast. Savitri tells him not to grieve. She says she started this observance with determination, and that same determination will carry it to completion. Your resolve for the GATE exam is real. The same force that set you on this path can see you through the daily start.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. You want to keep your feet on the ground after your best business year ever. Your grounded way of working now becomes the example your team and those around you will quietly follow.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna that people should act for the welfare of the world. Now Krishna explains why even those who have no personal need still keep working. He says that whatever a respected person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. The idea is that people imitate the conduct of those they look up to, so anyone with standing carries the weight of the example they leave behind. Your gratitude after a record year is real. Now the way you carry that success becomes the quiet rule your team and circle will copy.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel that everything is good and carry gratitude in your heart. Bhartrihari wonders at a life of simple freedom, honest food, good company, and a mind that stirs only gently. This quiet dignity you already hold is a rare blessing, the ripened fruit of great effort, to be wondered at rather than taken for granted.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva. He lists the quiet gifts of a simple life. He names freedom to move, food eaten with dignity, noble company, learning that brings calm, and a mind that stays gentle even when it looks outward. He wonders what generous austerity from the past could have produced such a life. He treats these plain goods as a rare blessing, not an ordinary right. You already hold this quiet dignity in your own retirement. What you feel as peace and gratitude is itself a rare ripened fruit, worthy of wonder rather than assumption.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You feel drawn to Krishna in a way you did not expect. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those seeking wealth, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among the welcome seekers, and that quiet pull you feel is already a form of devotion.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies, unsure whether to fight. Krishna has just said that the deluded and wrongdoers do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. In plain modern terms, whatever brings a person to the search matters less than the search itself. Distress, curiosity, need, and wisdom are four different doors. Your unexpected pull toward Krishna is not out of place. It is one of the four doors that Krishna names, and it already counts as a form of turning toward him.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You have found calm through meditation and chanting, and now you wish to go deeper toward God. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people worship him: those in distress, those curious, those in need, and those wise. Your path from peace into deeper devotion is one of those welcomed doors, and it already counts as good.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded and wrongdoers do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. He says the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise all worship him. He means that whatever brings a person to the search, whether trouble, curiosity, need, or wisdom, is welcome. All four are counted among the good. Your move from calm into deeper devotion is one of those welcomed doors, and it already counts as good.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You wish to feel that same joy in every moment. Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those seeking wealth, and the wise. Whatever door brings you close to God is welcome, including the simple longing to sing and feel that peace right now.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after noting that the deluded do not turn to him. He says that four kinds of good people worship him. These are the distressed, the curious, those in need, and the wise. He makes clear that any motive which brings a person toward the divine is accepted. The verse does not rank these seekers or demand a single pure reason. You already know the peace that rises when you sing. This verse says that same longing is enough to draw you near, whatever your reason may be today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: Karmaṇy evādhikāras te: your right is to the action. Fear of failure is a fear about the fruit, which was never given to you to control. Krishna also closes the escape route: don't let this make you stop acting. Care, prepare and aim well, then put the outcome down.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on a battlefield where the young warrior is frozen by dread. Arjuna fears the cost of fighting his own kin. Krishna tells him that a person has a right only to the action itself. The outcome belongs to no one who acts. Do the work with full attention. Do not let the craving for a particular result stop you from acting at all. Your launch is the work that belongs to you. The money that follows is not something you can hold in your hands. The fear lives in the gap between effort and outcome.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are carrying extra work after half the team was cut, waiting to see if you are next. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go; they do not last, so bear them. Right now, this uncertainty is a contact that will move on, not a permanent state. Let the extra tasks be what they are today, without deciding they will never end.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings come and go. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them patiently. What is truly real in a person outlasts every loss and every passing pain. The extra work and the waiting are contacts that come and go. They do not define what you are, and they are not permanent.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: Harsh words from your husband's family keep burning you, day after day. Krishna says his own heart is churned like a fire-stick by the harsh words his relatives speak. You do not have to carry that heat alone today; let the verse name the burn you already feel.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing tired of feuds inside his own clan. He tells Narada that he gives his relatives half of what he owns and bears their harsh words, yet those words still grind his heart like someone churning a fire-stick to keep a flame alive. The verse proposes that in family disputes the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect. Your husband's family pushed him to leave you because you could not give them a son. That rejection lands as a daily burn, and the verse names exactly that kind of wound from kin.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You carry the ache of missing your dad’s cremation. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is. Let this truth sit quietly beside your grief today, a steady presence that does not erase the loss, but remains.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving the prospect of fighting his own kin. Krishna tells him that the self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is slain. The verse proposes that whatever happens to the body, the self remains untouched by birth, growth, decay or death. It is unborn, eternal, constant and ancient. Your father's body reached India and was cremated while you were far away. This verse does not touch that distance. It points to what outlasts the body, and sits beside your ache without asking you to set it down.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: As we drop worn-out clothes and put on new ones, the self leaves a worn body for a new one.
verse_text.translation: Just as a person casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so the embodied self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the self casts off worn-out bodies and enters new ones, just as a person puts aside old clothes for fresh ones. You carry the ache of missing your father and not reaching his cremation in time. Let this image sit beside that loss: the body he lived in was set aside, while what mattered in him moved on.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Childhood, youth, old age: the body keeps changing. The wise aren't thrown by the next change.
verse_text.translation: Just as the embodied self passes through childhood, youth and old age in this body, so it passes on to another body. The steady person is not bewildered by this.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the embodied self passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, and then moves on to another body. The steady person is not bewildered by this. You have watched your dad move through his own life stages, and now you feel the weight of missing his final transition. The self remains unchanged through every stage, offering a ground to stand on beyond the loss.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: No weapon cuts it, no fire burns it, no water wets it, no wind dries it.
verse_text.translation: Weapons do not cut it, fire does not burn it, water does not wet it, and wind does not dry it.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that no weapon cuts the self, no fire burns it, no water wets it, and no wind dries it. This means whatever happened to the body at the end did not reach who your father truly was. You can stand on the fact that his essence remained beyond the reach of what occurred, even while the loss feels immense.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha on the fourth gatekeeper: good company (satsanga).
verse_text.line: Even at your lowest and most helpless, don't let go of good company.
verse_text.translation: Even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they should not let go of good company, not even a little.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama that even when people fall into the hardest straits and feel helpless, they must not let go of good company, not even a little. You are carrying the weight of missing your father's cremation, and isolation can feel like the only place left. Keeping one thread to a steady person—even for a few minutes—gives you ground to stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: A leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water: whatever is offered with love, I accept.
verse_text.translation: Whoever offers me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit or water, that offering of love from the pure-hearted I accept.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that he accepts a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or a little water whenever it is offered with love. You could place a single flower or a small bowl of water somewhere meaningful today, letting your love have a simple place to rest. This small act gives your heart a way to reach out without demanding anything in return.

story.title: Bharata returns to Ayodhya
story.summary: Bharata was far away at his grandfather's home when his father, King Dasharatha, died. Messengers called him back without telling him why. He rode into an Ayodhya that had gone quiet, went looking for his father, and learned he was gone. He fell to the ground and wept. When he could stand again, the family priest Vasishtha gently told him it was time to perform the last rites, and he did them, grieving as he went.
story.lesson: Missing the goodbye is its own grief. Let yourself feel it, then do what love asks next.

days.reading: Bharata rode back to Ayodhya to find his father Dasharatha already dead, and he wept on the ground before gently performing the last rites. You carry the ache of not reaching your dad in time for his cremation. Let that missing of the goodbye sit with you, and then move forward with whatever love asks of you next.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are stretched across office deadlines, your son's exam prep, and a toddler. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go; they do not last, so bear them. This restlessness can sit beside those demands without adding panic, knowing the pressure is a contact that moves on.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, right after explaining that the self moves through childhood, youth and old age. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These arrive and depart by nature. They do not last. So Arjuna must bear them without being swept away by either joy or grief. Your restlessness is one of those contacts. It moves through the office, the exam prep and the toddler. It does not last, and you do not have to let it carry you away.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: With work ramping up, a daycare calling about fever, and your partner away, you are caught in pressures that touch and move on. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go; they do not last, so bear them. Today, this means the fever call and the deadline are contacts that begin and end, not a body that must stand down forever. Let the daycare message pass through you like weather, and rest in the interval between one demand and the next.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield after Arjuna has laid down his weapons in grief. Arjuna is mourning the elders and kin he must fight. Krishna reminds him that the true self is never born and never dies, and that the body changes like clothes. Then he turns to the experiences that still sting while the self remains untouched. He says contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These arrive and depart by nature. They do not last. The pressure you carry right now is real, but it moves like weather across a sky that does not change.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You are starting your dream job on Monday, feeling excited yet terrified you will mess it up. Lakshmana tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. Your hope can hold both the thrill and the fear without choosing between them, letting that same energy carry you into the first day.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama is drowning in grief after Sita is taken. Every bird and mated deer around him only sharpens his longing. Lakshmana steps in and tells him that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it. For the person who has this energy, nothing in the world is out of reach. The point is that a friend can remind someone of their own strength when beauty deepens grief. Your hope for Monday can hold both the thrill and the fear without forcing you to pick one. That same energy can carry you through the door on your first day.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You have been going back and forth on leaving your job for months, and it occupies your thoughts day and night. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. When your thoughts keep circling the same decision, you are in the same company as the Gita’s finest archer, who named this storm honestly before any answer came.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has just heard that the highest person treats joy and pain as equal. Arjuna objects. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. It is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse takes this complaint seriously. It proposes that the mind is difficult to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it. Your mind is circling the same work decision because it is doing exactly what Arjuna described. The restlessness is not a signal that you are failing to decide.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You are moving through full-time work and raising two young children while your husband works nights, and the tiredness stays even on holidays. The Yoga Vasishtha says that a mind caught in endless waves of tasks—'done this, doing this, must do that'—never gets a moment's rest. Right now, that loop of reckoning may be exactly what you feel fraying; simply noticing the net of to-dos, without adding to it, can give the mind a small place to land.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa, whom he meets again as a grey-haired man after years apart. They had grown up together in a forest hermitage, then spent long lonely years in hard austerities after their fathers died. Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found peace. Bhasa answers that there is no wellness while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks and worries. He says the mind is carried along on great waves of tasks, never resting, its depths dancing with worry. Your tiredness staying through holidays fits this picture of a mind caught in endless waves of tasks rather than simple stress. The verse names the loop you are living, not a personal failing.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: You have a presentation tomorrow and keep imagining people laughing, thinking you do not belong in this course. Krishna tells Arjuna that your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits, and not to let that make you stop. You can still prepare your slides and show up fully, while letting the reaction of the room be something you do not carry alone.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is shaken and unsure whether to fight. Krishna tells him that a person has a right only to the action itself. The outcome belongs to no one. The work must be done fully. The result must not become the motive. Inaction is not the answer either. You can still prepare your slides and show up fully, while letting the reaction of the room be something you do not carry alone.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You are caught between bringing your widowed dad to Australia and moving back to be with him, knowing both paths cost someone something. Arjuna tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks plainly to be taught what is best. Your confusion today can be the honest starting point for seeking clarity, just as he laid his uncertainty before his teacher.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield and tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to tell him for certain what is best for him, offering himself as a student who has come to learn. You are facing a choice where both paths carry a real cost, and your own judgment feels too clouded to settle it yet.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You are caught between bringing your mother to you and returning to her alone in Patna. Arjuna tells Krishna his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks to be taught plainly what is best. Your own judgement feels clouded right now, and it is okay to admit you do not know the clear path forward. You can lay this uncertainty before someone you trust and simply ask to be shown the way.
meaning: Arjuna stands on the battlefield and tells Krishna that his nature is stricken by weakness and his mind is confused about what is right. He asks Krishna to tell him for certain what is best, saying he has come as a student to be taught. The verse proposes that clarity begins when a person admits their own judgement has failed and humbly asks for guidance rather than arguing for a choice already half made. Your own judgement feels clouded between bringing your mother here or going back to Patna alone, and it is okay to admit you do not know the clear path forward yet.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that you alone are the friend of yourself, and you alone are your own enemy. Right now, watching your batchmate’s promotion makes that inner voice feel harsh. You can choose to lift yourself up instead of pushing yourself down, and be the friend who encourages the next step forward.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You keep buying things and upgrading, yet nothing fills the space. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or any pleasure is to him, and who he really is. This verse meets that same restlessness by naming it as a true question, not a failure. Let the next phone or car rest for a moment, and sit with the question of who you are beneath the chase.
meaning: Young Rama has returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he seems so low. Rama answers that he no longer finds interest in his kingdom or in pleasure. He asks who he really is, and what all this is for. He wonders if the world is unreal, and if so, whose it is and who has truly gained anything. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your restlessness after each upgrade is the same question Rama voices. It is not a flaw in you. It is the start of a real inquiry into what you are chasing.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: After applying to 200 jobs since your company shut down, you have sat down with nothing. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. This verse names that exact moment of setting everything down when you cannot go on. The story does not end there; the next verses move toward asking for help and finding a way forward.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to Dhritarashtra, the blind king. He reports what has just happened on the battlefield. Arjuna has spoken of his fear and his grief. Now Arjuna puts down his bow and arrows. He sits on the seat of his chariot. His mind is overwhelmed. The verse names a moment when a strong person simply stops. It shows grief taking away the will to act. You have sent out two hundred applications since the company closed. You are sitting with the weight of that silence. This verse names the moment when a capable person simply stops.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You come home to an empty apartment, eat, and sleep, repeating the cycle with no one to share it with and no sense of what any of it is for. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure is to him, who he is, and what all this is for. This verse meets that same hollowness as a genuine doorway, not a flaw to fix, inviting you to sit with the question of what matters without forcing an answer today.
meaning: Young Rama has returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he looks so low. Rama answers by questioning everything around him. He asks what kingship or pleasure means to him. He asks who he really is and what all this is for. He suggests that if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your own cycle of coming home to silence and eating alone carries the same honest question. It is not a failure of will. It is the start of asking what matters.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You feel angry after your own nephew, whom you trained, took your biggest clients and opened his own shop. Bhartrihari cries out to hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart because he kept hoping for gain. Today, that same hope might be asking you how much longer you will keep dancing for people who took what was yours.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks to his own hope from the Censure of Craving. He tells it that he put up with the taunts of wicked people while trying to please them. He held back his tears and laughed with an empty heart. He even folded his hands before those numbed by money. He asks how much longer this hope will make him dance in humiliation. The verse names the cost of swallowing disrespect for the sake of gain. It carries that same cost into your own shop and the clients your nephew took.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: Your hands shook after the signal today. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, then desire, and then anger. This verse traces how anger can build from something the mind kept turning over before the outburst. You might notice the moment your mind starts dwelling on what irritates you, before the shouting begins.
meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna, who has asked what a person of steady mind looks like in speech and bearing. Krishna explains that when someone dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and when that desire meets an obstacle, it turns into anger. This is how steadiness is lost, not by a single sudden blow, but by the mind returning again and again to what it fixates on. Your shouting at the signal did not appear from nowhere. It grew from a mind that had already been turning over the irritations of the road, building a craving that snapped when the other driver did not move.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You notice irritation building fast these days. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person keeps dwelling on objects, attachment is born, then desire, and then anger. That means the flare-up you feel may trace back to something you have been turning over in your mind. You might try noticing the moment your thoughts settle on a trigger, before the snap arrives.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna asks what a person of steady wisdom looks like in speech, sitting and walking. Krishna has just warned that the senses can carry away even a wise person's mind. Now he traces the inner path. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding attention, because anger starts with what you dwell on. The irritation you feel may trace back to something you have been turning over in your mind. The flare-up is not the first moment.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You are running your own thing yet a small mistake by staff leaves you fuming all day. Bhartrihari tells the reader that serving a master means any behaviour is read as a fault: quiet and you are dull, patient and you are weak. This verse names that bind. Today, your anger may be touching that same impossible position, where any response gets twisted. You might anchor instead in your own standard of how the shop ought to run.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from his Nitishatakam, in the section on wicked people. He is describing the courtier who serves a cruel master. No matter what the servant does, the master twists it into a fault. Stay silent and you are dull. Speak and you are a show-off. Stay close and you are pushy. Keep away and you lack confidence. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse to endure and you are ill bred. The duty of serving another is a deep bind. Even yogis with their great insight cannot fully fathom it. You run your own shop, yet a small staff error leaves you fuming all day. The verse names a bind where any response gets twisted, and your anger may be touching that same impossible position.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You wake up replaying how loud you got when your partner broke your agreement. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and holding it feels like holding the wind. When your thoughts race like that at night, you are naming a real struggle that even the Gita's hero admitted aloud. Let the image of the wind remind you that this restlessness is not a quiet failure, but a force that is simply hard to hold.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after hearing that a yogi sees all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last because the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that the mind is difficult to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it. Your mind races back to the moment your partner broke the agreement and your temper rose. That replay at night is the restlessness Arjuna names, and it is hard to hold without training.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You are angry after throwing your phone at the wall because your roommate used your stuff. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person keeps dwelling on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, then anger. Right now, your mind may have been turning over that boundary for a while before it flared. The verse simply traces how dwelling hardens into wanting, and wanting that meets a wall becomes anger.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna what a person of steady mind looks like in speech and conduct. Krishna answers that when someone dwells on objects, attachment is born. From that attachment comes desire, and when desire is blocked, it turns into anger. Your anger at your roommate may have been building from dwelling on that boundary before it finally flared.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You grip the steering wheel until your hands ache because anything slowing you down makes you boil. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, which blocked turns into anger. Today, the traffic itself may just be traffic, yet the heat you feel can point to what you have been turning over and needing to move forward. Notice the wheel under your palms as a signal to loosen your hold, even for a moment.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna asks what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna has just warned that the senses can carry away even a wise man. Now he traces the inner chain. A person dwells on objects and forms attachment to them. That attachment hardens into wanting. When that wanting meets a block, it turns into anger and ruin. The heat in traffic may be pointing to something you have been turning over and needing to move forward, not merely the cars ahead of you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: When a client changes the brief at the last minute, you see red and fire off emails you later have to apologise for. Krishna tells Arjuna that dwelling on objects breeds attachment, attachment turns into desire, and blocked desire becomes anger. The verse points to the moment before the flare, when the mind keeps turning the brief over and over. You might notice the tightness in your jaw as a signal to step back, before the next email goes out.
meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna, who has asked what a person of steady mind looks like. Krishna traces how the mind lands on an object and dwells there. That dwelling breeds attachment. The attachment hardens into wanting. When that wanting meets a block, it turns into anger. The verse proposes that steadiness comes from guarding where the attention rests. Your anger at the late brief has a quieter start, before the email is sent. The verse points to the moment your mind keeps turning the request over and over.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You spoke about anger taking over in the moment and the awkwardness that followed. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. This verse names the struggle you are living now: the gap between the person you want to be and the harsh words that came out anyway.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their own will, as if pushed by some outside force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this anger is the true enemy that clouds a person's wisdom like smoke hiding a fire. The verse proposes that you can master this force once you see it clearly.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
