verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: At work, a small thing sets you off and you look away. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born; from attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. This points to the moment before the flare, when something keeps turning over in your mind. You might notice the breath right before you snap, and simply let the gaze rest there.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has asked what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna answers by tracing a chain. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. At work, a small thing sets you off and you look away. The flare may start earlier, in a thought you kept turning over before the moment.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?

reading: Krishna starts earlier than the outburst. Dhyāyato viṣayān puṃsaḥ: when you keep dwelling on something, you get attached, attachment turns into wanting, and wanting that meets a wall turns into anger. By the time you snap, the fire has been building for a while.

verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You feel uneasy about losing your cool with delivery guys and waiters. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, which turns into anger. This suggests the flare-up may follow a quiet moment of fixating on what you want. Notice the pause before the snap, and let your next breath rest there.
meaning: Krishna answers Arjuna, who has just asked what a person of steady mind looks like in speech and bearing. Krishna traces a chain. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding attention, because anger starts with what you dwell on. The flare you feel with delivery workers and waiters may follow a quiet moment when you fixated on how a service ought to go.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: Krishna starts earlier than the outburst. Dhyāyato viṣayān puṃsaḥ: when you keep dwelling on something, you get attached, attachment turns into wanting, and wanting that meets a wall turns into anger. By the time you snap, the fire has been building for a while.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has just asked what a person of steady mind looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna answers by tracing a chain. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire, when it is blocked, anger arises. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding attention, because anger starts with what you dwell on rather than with the final insult. You told me you need anger management. This verse does not judge your anger. It shows that the fire often starts earlier, in the moments you keep turning something over in your mind.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: The narrator Sanjaya speaks these words. He describes the greatest archer of his time putting down his bow and sitting in the chariot, his mind sunk in sorrow. The Gita begins with someone who can't go on, and it stays with him for seventeen more chapters.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna has just argued that killing his own kin is worse than death. Overcome by grief and fear, Arjuna drops his bow and arrows and sits down in his chariot. He cannot move. The verse marks this collapse. It shows that even the strongest person can freeze when sorrow takes over. The teaching begins here, with this breakdown, not with a hero ready to fight. You are watching others move ahead while you carry the load alone in a spare room. That gap can feel like proof that you have stopped. The verse names exactly that freeze, without calling it final.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: You feel the sting when you see your former juniors reach the top. Bhartrihari tells the reader that in serving a master, silence makes you dull and speech makes you a show-off; patience is weakness and refusal is ill-bred. The verse speaks to you today by naming the double bind you are caught in, where any path looks like a fault. You can anchor in your own standard rather than searching for a single right behaviour that will finally be seen.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from his Nitishatakam, in the section on wicked people. He is describing the impossible position of anyone who serves a master. The master turns every behaviour into a fault. Silence makes you dull. Speech makes you a show-off. Patience makes you weak. Refusal makes you ill bred. Serving another is a duty so deep that even yogis cannot fathom it.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he seems so low. Rama answers that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him, who he really is, and what all this is for. If the world is unreal, let it be unreal. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your emptiness right now is not a failure. It is the first honest question about what you want next, after the noise of comparison has worn off.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: You notice the other mums at school pickup with careers and homes, while you gave yours up and feel behind. Krishna says it is better to walk your own path, even imperfectly, than to perform another's duty well. Your choice to raise your children is your own duty lived honestly, not a copy of anyone else's life.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield as Arjuna hesitates to fight. Krishna tells him that each person has a duty suited to their own nature. It is better to do your own work, even if you do it imperfectly, than to perform someone else's duty perfectly. When you act from your own nature, you do not incur fault. Your choice to raise your children is your own duty lived honestly, not a copy of anyone else's life. The feeling of being behind comes from measuring your path against theirs.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: At every family dinner, you are the other one while your sister’s path shines ahead. Krishna tells Arjuna that doing one’s own duty, even imperfectly, is better than another’s done perfectly. Your studies have their own worth, and walking them honestly counts more than copying a highlight reel that was never yours to run.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna that perfection comes from worshipping through his own work. Now Krishna says that one's own duty, even if done imperfectly, is better than another's duty performed perfectly. Doing work that fits one's own nature brings no fault. The idea is to act from one's own makeup rather than copying another person's role. Your studies have their own worth, and walking them honestly counts more than copying a highlight reel that was never yours to run.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse_text.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that doing your own duty, even imperfectly, is better than doing another's perfectly, and that borrowing someone else's path brings fear. The verse sees comparison as a quiet swap that replaces your own way with another's and then judges you by their measure. In your family dinners, the spotlight on your sister's achievement can feel like pressure to live her story; the Gita simply holds that your own path, however uneven right now, is the safer ground.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how the wise live and work.
verse_text.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
verse_text.translation: Content with whatever comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, even when acting he is not bound.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise stay content with what arrives unasked, steady through success and failure, and free from envy even while working. You can keep your own path without glancing sideways at your sister's achievements. Let today's ground be simply resting in what has come to you, acting steadily, and staying even when outcomes differ.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Drop the cravings, the sense of 'mine' and the 'I' that keeps score. That's where peace is.
verse_text.translation: The person who gives up all desires and moves about free from longing, without the sense of 'mine' and without ego, attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to drop cravings, the sense of 'mine', and the 'I' that keeps score, because that is where peace is. At every family dinner, the room seems to measure you against her path. You can move through that same table without letting an inner scorekeeper rank your worth against hers.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to lift himself up and not push himself down, because the self alone is both friend and enemy. When you measure yourself against your sister at family dinners, that inner voice can become your own worst enemy. You could try speaking to yourself today the way you would to a friend who is struggling, offering one encouraging word instead of the next comparison.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Doing your own work well can be your worship of the source of all life.
verse_text.translation: By worshipping, through his own work, Him from whom all beings arise and by whom all this is pervaded, a person attains perfection.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that doing your own work well, and worshipping through it the source of all life, brings perfection. You could treat one task today—your studying or a small duty—as that offering, letting it stand on its own without measuring it against your sister's path. The work itself becomes the point, not a rank.

story.title: The mongoose and the handful of flour
story.summary: At the end of Yudhishthira's grand horse sacrifice, a mongoose appeared with one side of its body made of gold. It declared that the whole sacrifice was worth less than a handful of flour. Once, it said, during a famine, a poor gleaner and his family each gave their last share of flour to a hungry guest. When the mongoose rolled in the flour that had spilled, half its body turned gold. It had gone to many great sacrifices since, hoping to turn the other half, and none had done it.
story.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.

days.reading: At the end of Yudhishthira's grand sacrifice, a mongoose with half its body turned gold declared that a poor family's small handful of flour given to a hungry guest outweighed the entire ritual. This speaks to you because it measures worth by honest giving from little, not by grand outcomes or others' medals. Your own small, honest step today is enough.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.

verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: Your brother’s shop runs twice as fast, and relatives count it at every wedding. Krishna says it is better to walk your own path, even imperfectly, than to perform someone else’s duty well. Your own work has its own weight, and it stands on its own without copying his pace.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after listing the duties tied to different ways of life. He tells him that perfection comes from doing one's own work as an offering. Then he repeats that one's own path, walked with all its flaws, beats another person's path done perfectly. Acting in line with what fits you naturally does not bring fault. Your brother's shop moves faster, and relatives measure it against yours at every wedding. The verse asks you to see your own work as having its own weight, separate from his pace.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: You moved away seeking a better life, yet find yourself measuring your path against friends who stayed behind. Krishna tells Arjuna that doing one's own duty, even imperfectly, is better than another's well performed. Your own journey abroad holds its own worth, separate from how comfortably others live near home.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna stands between two armies, unsure whether to fight. Krishna has been teaching him about action and duty. Here he says that each person has work suited to their own nature. Doing that work, even if it is flawed, is better than performing another person's duty perfectly. Acting in line with your own nature brings no fault. Your move for a better life is its own honest work. The discomfort you feel now comes from measuring it against a comfort you did not choose.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that doing your own duty, even imperfectly, is better than another’s done perfectly. When comparison is killing your peace, this points to the quiet truth that your own path counts, however messy it looks next to others. You can let that truth sit with you today, and return to your own work without measuring it against anyone else's finish line.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is caught between two armies and unsure whether to take up arms. Krishna tells him that each person has duties that fit their own nature. Doing your own work, even with flaws, is better than copying another person and doing it perfectly. Acting in line with who you are does not bring fault. Your comparison is eating at the peace you have built through your own work. This points to the quiet truth that your path counts, however messy it looks next to others.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse_text.line: Better your own path done imperfectly than someone else's done perfectly. Borrowed lives are dangerous.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, even done imperfectly, than the duty of another well done. Better is death in one's own duty; the duty of another is full of fear.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that doing your own duty, even imperfectly, is better than another’s done perfectly, and that borrowing another’s path brings fear. When comparison quietly swaps your path for someone else’s, you end up graded by standards that are not yours. Today, notice one moment when you measure yourself against a friend’s or batchmate’s success, and gently return to the task in front of you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how the wise live and work.
verse_text.line: Content with what comes, beyond envy, steady in success and failure, you stay free even while working.
verse_text.translation: Content with whatever comes unasked, beyond the pairs of opposites, free from envy, the same in success and failure, even when acting he is not bound.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise stay content with what comes unasked, free from envy, steady in success and failure, and remain unbound even while working. This speaks to your anxious restlessness by offering ground to stand on: your peace does not depend on measuring up to others. You can keep moving through your own work while letting go of the sideways glance.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Drop the cravings, the sense of 'mine' and the 'I' that keeps score. That's where peace is.
verse_text.translation: The person who gives up all desires and moves about free from longing, without the sense of 'mine' and without ego, attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to drop desires, the sense of 'mine', and the 'I' that keeps score, so peace can come. You feel comparison is killing your peace. The scorekeeper in your mind ranks you against others all day. Loosening its grip on what you have, without dropping your people, gives you ground to stand on right now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to lift himself up by his own effort and not let himself sink, because the self alone is the friend of the self and the enemy of the self. When comparison turns into harsh self-talk, you could notice which voice you are following right now and gently choose to encourage yourself instead of pushing yourself down. You might speak to yourself as you would to a friend who is struggling, taking one small step forward today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Doing your own work well can be your worship of the source of all life.
verse_text.translation: By worshipping, through his own work, Him from whom all beings arise and by whom all this is pervaded, a person attains perfection.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that doing your own work well, as an offering to the source of all life, is itself worship and brings perfection. You could treat one task today as your own offering, without measuring it against anyone else's path. This keeps the work yours, not a borrowed life.

story.title: The mongoose and the handful of flour
story.summary: At the end of Yudhishthira's grand horse sacrifice, a mongoose appeared with one side of its body made of gold. It declared that the whole sacrifice was worth less than a handful of flour. Once, it said, during a famine, a poor gleaner and his family each gave their last share of flour to a hungry guest. When the mongoose rolled in the flour that had spilled, half its body turned gold. It had gone to many great sacrifices since, hoping to turn the other half, and none had done it.
story.lesson: A small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show.

days.reading: A mongoose with half its body turned to gold declares that Yudhishthira’s grand sacrifice was worth less than a poor family’s handful of flour given in famine. The story shows that a small gift, honestly earned and given from little, outweighs the grandest show. When comparison pulls at your peace, this points to the quiet worth already present in your own efforts, not the scale of anyone else’s offering.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, who has collapsed in tears on the battlefield and refuses to fight.
verse_text.line: I'm confused about what's right. Tell me plainly what's best; I'm ready to learn.
verse_text.translation: My nature is stricken by weakness and my mind is confused about what is right. I ask you: tell me for certain what is best for me. I am your student; I have come to you, teach me.

reading: You face a deposit deadline in ten days and cannot tell whether to go abroad or keep your job. Arjuna tells Krishna that his mind is confused about what is right, and he asks plainly to be taught what is best. Your own uncertainty does not mean your care is wrong; it simply names the moment where you stop arguing and let a clearer voice meet the choice before you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are caught between two jobs and two cities, unsure which path is right. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact with the world brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and these come and go. You can notice this push and pull as something that arrives and moves on, without letting it sweep you away.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving the prospect of fighting his own kin. Krishna tells him that the self within never dies and never is born. verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people come to the divine: the distressed, the curious, the needy, and the wise. reading: You want to surrender to God. Krishna tells Arjuna that people come to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and calls all four kinds good. Your turn toward the divine is already counted among what is welcome. You can let that openness shape how you pray today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that the deluded and wrongdoers do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. These are the distressed, the curious, those in need, and the wise. He says all four kinds worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search is welcome. You want to surrender to God. Your turn toward the divine is already counted among what is welcome.

reading: You find peace walking into the mandir and wish to feel closer to Kanha. The curious come to know. The needy come for help. The wise come from steady understanding. All four are counted as good. Your wish to draw nearer to Kanha is already a form of turning. It does not need to be earned by a single motive.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits, and he adds not to let that make you stop. In your mock interviews this week, the blanking you feel belongs to the result, which was never yours to hold. Let your attention rest on the next question you answer, and put the final round down.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has laid down his weapons and said he will not fight. Krishna tells him to do his work fully and let go of owning what comes after. In plain modern words, you have a right to the action itself, not to what it produces. Do not let the fear of the outcome keep you from acting at all. Your mock interviews belong to the work, not to the offer letter that may follow. The blanking you feel is the result trying to take over the room.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You have a big investor pitch next Tuesday, and you rehearse every night yet still feel you will freeze in front of them. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Your mind tonight is that wind, and naming it honestly is the first step toward steadying it before the meeting.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi as one who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such steady evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna agrees that the mind is difficult to steady, but he answers that practice and letting go can train it. Your mind tonight is that wind. Naming the restlessness honestly, before the pitch, is the first step toward steadying it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You sat on the floor crying with thankfulness as your son took his first steps. The poet wonders at a life of simple freedom, honest food, good company, and a mind that stirs only gently. Today, that same wonder can meet you in this exact moment, as you hold the quiet gift of his new beginning.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines from his Worship of Shiva to anyone who reads them. He has just noted that moonlight, poetry and good company lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are, and that the wise leave palaces for the forest. He then lists the goods of a simple life. You are sitting in the middle of raising children and feeling the weight of ordinary miracles. The poet asks what earned him this simple freedom, and you can wonder at the dignity already present in your own days.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: The self was never born and never dies. It is not killed when the body is.
verse_text.translation: It is never born and never dies; having been, it will not cease to be. Unborn, eternal, constant and ancient, it is not slain when the body is slain.

reading: You still make your amma’s dal and cry into the pot. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. That truth can sit beside your grief today, not above it, as the same dal you stir holds both her memory and your sorrow.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is shaken by the thought of fighting his own kin. Krishna tells him that the self was never born and never dies. It remains constant and ancient. The body may be slain, but the self is not killed. Your amma's body has passed, yet the truth she was at her core was never born and will not end. That can sit beside your sorrow without erasing it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.

reading: You are carrying the sudden silence of your father’s passing, and now your children ask where Nana went. Your father's body is gone, yet what he most deeply was remains untouched by that loss.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You now drink your morning chai alone. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. When the house feels quiet, this can mean that no distance or silence can fully separate you from what surrounds you. The cup in your hand and the morning air can hold that closeness today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him how to settle the mind through meditation. He has just described the yogi who sees the self in all beings. Now he speaks in the first person. He says that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him is never out of his sight, and he is never out of that person's sight. The morning quiet after your wife passed six months ago still holds a presence that does not turn away from you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna

reading: You feel empty as uni carries on like nothing happened after your best mate died. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. Let that truth sit beside the grief today, not replacing it, as you walk through campus.

It does not end when the body ends. The self simply outlasts every change that bodies go through. Your best mate is gone from this world, and the self that was in them was never born to die. verse_text.speaker: Krishna

meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving the death of his kin and does not want to fight. Krishna tells him that the self was never born and never dies. It does not cease to be when the body ends. The self is unborn, eternal, constant and ancient. It is not slain when the body is slain. Your brother's body has ended, but the verse speaks of what in him was never born and never dies. That thought can sit quietly beside the sorrow you hold for him and his children.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna

reading: You are back at work after ten days away, acting normal. Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is. This speaks to you today as a quiet truth sitting beside your grief: the core of your father was never born and will not end with his body. Let that remain near you as you move through your day.

Your father's body has ended, but the core of who he was was never born and will not end with it. That truth can sit beside your grief without asking you to set it down.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You still set out two cups for tea every morning. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else can know this ache; only the heart knows the love it misses. That private weight you carry each dawn is seen. Let the second cup stand as it does, a quiet witness to what your heart alone holds.
meaning: Ram sends this message to Sita through Hanuman. Sita sits captive in the grove, threatened by Ravana, and has nearly lost hope. Hanuman has already told her Ram's story and dropped Ram's ring from the tree. Now Ram says that speaking of pain lightens it a little. But there is no one to tell, because no one else knows this ache. Only the heart that loves knows the truth of that love and the depth of what is missed. The morning ritual with the two cups holds a love that no one else can fully know. Ram's words name the loneliness of carrying that private weight alone.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.

Krishna tells Arjuna that the self was never born and never dies; it is not slain when the body is slain. verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You took money from your parents' savings for your startup and lost it, and their silence weighs on you. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if pushed by force. That question names the ache of a choice you cannot undo, without judging the person behind it. You can sit with that question as it is, right alongside the quiet that still surrounds you.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person commits wrongdoing even when it goes against their own will, as if some outside force is pushing them. Krishna answers that desire which is blocked turns into anger, and this desire is the enemy that clouds a person's wisdom like smoke covering a fire. The verse proposes that a person can see this pattern clearly and then master it.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.

verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You carry the memory of firing someone years ago and hearing he struggled since. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their will, as if forced by something outside. The verse names that inner pull without calling you wicked or excusing the harm. You can sit with that question today, letting the verse hold the weight of what happened, rather than letting it define you.

You carry the memory of firing someone in anger and hearing he struggled long after. The verse names the inner pull that drove that moment without calling you wicked or excusing the harm.

This verse names the struggle you live inside, not to condemn you, but to meet it with honesty. The question itself is the first step toward understanding what happened.

Your regret names a struggle you live inside, where part of you wants one thing and another part acts against it. The verse meets that split with honesty, not to condemn you, but to help you see the pattern clearly.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You carry the weight of a lie that brought you this job, and each day feels like theft. Manu speaks of a poor man who finds the wishing tree yet hesitates to ask, not knowing its power. Your doubt about deserving this place may be hiding the truth that the one who placed you here is far more generous than you assume.
meaning: King Manu speaks to Lord Vishnu after years of austerity. Vishnu appears and tells him to ask any boon. Manu says that seeing the Lord's feet already fulfils every wish, yet one great longing remains. He compares himself to a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power. The verse proposes that it is not too late to turn toward what matters, but it takes courage to ask for it.

Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this anger is the enemy that clouds wisdom like smoke over fire. He tells Arjuna to master it by seeing it clearly. You are asking why the year of silence happened even though a part of you did not want it. The verse says the force was desire, and now it has turned into anger that clouds your judgment.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: Even if you were the worst wrongdoer of all, the raft of wisdom would carry you across.
verse_text.translation: Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners, you will cross over all wrongdoing by the raft of knowledge alone.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that even if you were the worst wrongdoer of all, the raft of knowledge would carry you across. This speaks to the weight you feel when kindness meets what you did years ago. The verse sees that weight as a river behind you, not the final place you stand. You can cross over from it, while the river still remains.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the power of understanding to end confusion and guilt.
verse_text.line: As a blazing fire turns wood to ash, real understanding burns away the hold of past actions.
verse_text.translation: As a blazing fire reduces fuel to ashes, Arjuna, so the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that real understanding burns away the hold of past actions, just as a blazing fire turns wood to ash. The affair happened, and its weight still presses on you when your wife is kind. Knowledge does not erase what already began, yet it can loosen the grip of replaying that choice, giving you ground to stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: Even if you've done great wrong, the moment you turn wholeheartedly, count yourself among the good.
verse_text.translation: Even if one of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, he should be regarded as good, for he has resolved rightly.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that even someone who has done great wrong, the moment they turn wholeheartedly, should be regarded as good because their resolve is right. Your past does not lock the door on where you stand now. You can count yourself among the good today, not because the harm vanished, but because your resolve to face it is finally right.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on simple, wholehearted devotion.
verse_text.line: Such a person soon turns good and finds lasting peace. Mark it: no one devoted to me is ever lost.
verse_text.translation: He soon becomes righteous and attains lasting peace. Kaunteya, declare it boldly: my devotee never perishes.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that someone who turns wholeheartedly soon becomes righteous and finds lasting peace, and that his devotee is never lost. You carry the weight of an old choice even though your wife has shown kindness since. You could let one small act of honest care today be the first step toward becoming someone at peace with himself.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna's final counsel: act with devotion, reflect, choose, and take refuge.
verse_text.line: Lean on me alone. I will free you from every wrong. Don't worry.
verse_text.translation: Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone. I will free you from all sins; do not grieve.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to abandon all reliance on his own efforts and take refuge in him alone, promising to free him from every wrong and telling him not to grieve. You could try setting the weight of that old choice down for a moment today, trusting that you do not have to carry the burden of perfect repair by yourself. Then you can meet your wife's kindness without the constant pressure to earn it.

story.title: Yudhishthira after the war
story.summary: Yudhishthira won the war and could not bear it. So many of his own family were dead, and he blamed himself. He wanted to give up the throne and go into the forest for good. One after another, his brothers, Draupadi, and the sages Devasthana and Vyasa argued with him about duty, guilt, grief and the shortness of life. Slowly he agreed to stay and rule, and to spend what was left of his life doing good.
story.lesson: Guilt and grief are real, but they are not the end. The good you do next counts.

days.reading: Yudhishthira won the war yet felt crushed by guilt over his dead kin, and he wanted to disappear into the forest. Like you carrying the weight of a past choice you cannot undo, his story shows that guilt can feel overwhelming even after victory. Yet he stayed to rule and do good, so your next kind act toward your wife can be the place where you simply remain.

verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their own will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this desire is the enemy that clouds wisdom like smoke over fire. The verse proposes that a person can master this force by seeing it clearly. You asked what drives someone to hurt another even when they do not want to. The text says the force is desire that has turned sour, and it can be seen and handled.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You have felt weeks of steady calm, where traffic and deadlines no longer get under your skin. Krishna tells Arjuna that one whose happiness, delight and light are all within finds lasting freedom. This points to a steadiness that does not rely on things going your way, so you might rest in the calm you already carry, letting it be enough today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly. He describes the wise person who treats all beings with an equal eye. This person is not elated by gain nor crushed by loss. Their happiness, delight and light all come from within. Because they see that sense pleasures begin and end in sorrow, they withstand desire and anger. Such a yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman while still living on earth. You have already tasted this steadiness, and the verse names the source you can rest in today.

reading: Krishna describes someone whose happiness, pleasure and light are all inside: antaḥ-sukhaḥ, antar-ārāmaḥ, antar-jyotiḥ. Good days still come from outside. This joy doesn't depend on them.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna sorts knowledge, action, doers, judgement, resolve and happiness by the three qualities.
verse_text.line: Some pleasure tastes like nectar at first and poison in the end. Know which kind you're choosing.
verse_text.translation: The happiness that comes from contact of the senses with their objects, like nectar at first and like poison in the end, is called rajasic.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that pleasure born when the senses meet their objects tastes like nectar at first, yet becomes like poison in the end. Since you feel a quiet joy within and wish to know it more deeply, this points to the difference between outer stimulation and the lasting calm you already carry. Notice which kind of sweetness your attention reaches for today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Unhooked from outside pleasures, you find a joy within that doesn't run out.
verse_text.translation: One whose self is unattached to outer contacts finds the happiness that is in the self. Joined to Brahman by yoga, he enjoys undying happiness.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when the mind is unhooked from outer contacts, it finds a joy within that does not run out. You already feel an inner delight and want to know it more deeply. This verse gives you ground to stand on: the gladness you sense is not waiting on anything outside you to keep going.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: When the mind clears, sorrows start to dissolve, and understanding settles quickly.
verse_text.translation: In that clarity all sorrows come to an end; for one whose mind is clear, understanding soon becomes steady.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that when the mind clears, sorrows begin to dissolve, and understanding settles quickly. You feel a peaceful ease within and want to know it more deeply. As your mind grows clearer, sorrows loosen their hold on their own, and a steady understanding takes root. Let this clarity be the ground you stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna sorts knowledge, action, doers, judgement, resolve and happiness by the three qualities.
verse_text.line: Some joy tastes like poison at first and like nectar in the end. That joy is worth it.
verse_text.translation: That which is like poison at first and like nectar in the end, born from the clarity of one's own understanding, is called sattvic happiness.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that some joy tastes like poison at first yet becomes nectar in the end, born from a clear mind. You could sit quietly today and notice one small habit that feels effortful, letting its quiet sweetness gather without forcing it. This is the steady joy you sensed within, ripening simply as you return to it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on three kinds of food, effort, speech and giving.
verse_text.line: A calm mind, gentleness, quiet, self-restraint and a clean heart: that is discipline of mind.
verse_text.translation: Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint and purity of feeling: this is called austerity of the mind.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a calm mind, gentleness, quiet, self-restraint and a clean heart make up the discipline of the mind. Since you already feel a peaceful joy within and wish to know it more deeply, you could sit quietly for a few minutes today and notice any harsh thought before it becomes a word. Let your heart stay open and sincere as you rest in that inner light.

story.title: Bhushunda
story.summary: The sage Vasishtha travelled to a wish-fulfilling tree on Mount Meru to meet Bhushunda, a crow who had watched whole ages of the world come and go and was still happy. Asked his secret, Bhushunda listed his habits. He didn't brood on the past or the future. He didn't fret about what he'd get next. Learning never made him proud. And he was glad when others were glad, and sad when they were sad.
story.lesson: A long, glad life comes from staying present, wanting little and staying kind.

days.reading: Bhushunda the crow, who outlived whole ages, told Vasishtha he stayed happy by not brooding on the past or future, fretting over what comes next, or growing proud from learning. This speaks to your peaceful, retired stage, where an inner delight already lives. Let his habit of remaining present and kind guide how you sit with this joy today.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You are in a gap year at home with your grandparents and have never felt this calm. The poet wonders at his own freedom to wander, honest food, good company, and a mind that stirs only gently. You can carry this same wonder into the next chapter, holding onto the quiet dignity of this season as a rare blessing rather than a pause before the rush.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks these lines to the reader from his section on the worship of Shiva. He has just noted that moonlight, poetry and good company lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are. Here he lists the goods of a simple, even ascetic, life. He names freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, and learning whose only fruit is calm. He says his mind stirs only gently even when he looks outward for long. He wonders what generous austerity has ripened into this blessing.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Eating alone in the dining hall most days while everyone else sits in their groups, you may feel unseen. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him in everything and everything in him is never lost to him, and he is never lost to them. This means that even across the distance from home, a bond remains that no table of strangers can break. You can carry that awareness with you into the hall tomorrow.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just described the yogi who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. Now he restates this in his own voice. He says that one who sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him is never out of his sight, and he is never out of that person's sight. The verse proposes that a settled mind comes from moderation and from gently returning attention again and again, so that separation does not take hold. Across the distance from home, a bond remains that no table of strangers can break.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You stay at home while your husband works long hours, and some days pass without you speaking to another adult. Krishna tells Arjuna, "See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me." This means that even on the quietest days, you are not unseen or cast away. You might notice this bond in the ordinary moments around you—a shared glance, a routine task—where you feel held rather than alone.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while teaching him about meditation and a settled mind. Arjuna has been asking how one can keep the mind steady. Krishna replies that whoever sees the divine presence in all things and sees all things resting within that presence will never be separated from it. The divine will never lose sight of that person either. You are in a new country with small children and long hours between you and your husband. This verse says that even when no adult speaks to you, you remain held in a bond that does not break.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna where the divine is found.
verse_text.line: The divine lives in the heart of every being, yours included.
verse_text.translation: The Lord dwells in the heart of every being, Arjuna, moving all beings by his power as if mounted on a machine.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the Lord dwells in the heart of every being, including yours, right here in this flat and this city. Because the divine lives inside you, you are never empty or wholly alone, even on days when no adult speaks to you. Let this presence be the ground you stand on today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna tells Arjuna who he is to every being.
verse_text.line: I am your goal, your support, your witness, your home, your shelter and your friend.
verse_text.translation: I am the goal, the sustainer, the master, the witness, the home, the refuge and the friend; the origin and the dissolution, the ground, the treasure-house and the undying seed.

days.reading: In one verse Krishna lists what he is to every being: goal, support, witness, home (nivāsaḥ), shelter (śaraṇam) and friend (suhṛt). If you've been missing all of those, this verse names them together.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, briefly describing meditation and the peace it brings.
verse_text.line: The divine is the well-wisher of every being, you included. Knowing this, you find peace.
verse_text.translation: Knowing me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the great lord of all the worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the divine is the selfless friend and well-wisher of every being, and knowing this brings peace. You may spend days without speaking to another adult, yet this verse presents a presence that wishes you well without expecting anything in return. Let that steady companionship ground you this evening, even when the house stays quiet.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Feel others' joy and pain as if they were your own. That is the highest practice.
verse_text.translation: One who, by comparison with himself, sees the same everywhere, Arjuna, whether in pleasure or in pain, is considered the highest yogi.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to feel others' joy and pain as if they were his own; that is the highest practice. You could try this today by noticing one small thing—a smile or a struggle—in someone around you, and letting it register as your own. This turns your attention outward, where connection often begins.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, describing the qualities of the person dear to God.
verse_text.line: Hate no one. Be friendly and kind, free of 'mine' and ego, steady in pain and joy, and forgiving.
verse_text.translation: One who hates no being, who is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and ego, even in pain and pleasure, and forgiving,

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the one dear to God hates no one, is friendly and compassionate, free from possessiveness and ego, steady through pain and joy, and forgiving. Since some days pass without you speaking to another adult, you could offer a small kindness to someone today—a smile, a brief chat, or a helping hand—without expecting anything in return. You can choose to be the friendly one first, even when nothing comes back right away.

story.title: Ram and Sugriva become friends
story.summary: Ram had lost his home, and his wife Sita had been taken. Sugriva, driven out by his brother, had lost his home and his wife too. They met in the forest and swore friendship before a fire. Then Sugriva brought out the jewels Sita had dropped as she was carried away. Ram broke down at the sight of them, and Sugriva, who had his own grief, comforted him: in trouble, think it through steadily, and lean on your friend.
story.lesson: Two people in trouble can carry each other.

days.reading: In the Kishkindha Kanda, Ram and Sugriva, both driven from home and grieving their lost wives, meet in the forest and swear friendship before a fire. Sugriva then returns Sita’s dropped jewels, and though he carries his own sorrow, he comforts Ram to think steadily and lean on a friend. On days when you do not speak to another adult, this shows that two people in trouble can carry each other.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: With both sons settled away and the two of you here alone, days feel endless. Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever sees him in everything and everything in him is never lost to him, nor he to them. You might notice the familiar in a neighbour's greeting or the street outside your window, letting that presence stay close without replacing the company you miss.
meaning: Krishna speaks this to Arjuna while teaching him about meditation and a settled mind. Arjuna has been listening to how a yogi should live. Krishna says that a person who sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him will never be lost to him, and he will never be lost to that person.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: Three years at home have left you with no one around, and your phone only buzzes for work. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure is to him, and who he really is, and what all this is for. story.title: Satyakama Jabala
story.summary: Young Satyakama wanted to study, but he didn't know his father's lineage. He told the teacher exactly what his mother had told him. reading: Your shoulders are up by your ears with midterms, work shifts and club deadlines. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy and as hard to hold as the wind. Right now your thoughts may feel just as stubborn and strong, refusing to settle even when your body wants to rest.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes a yogi who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last. The mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. It is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that this difficulty is real, yet practice and letting go can train the mind. Your mind is caught between midterms, shifts and deadlines. It feels as hard to steady as the wind right now.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Your inbox keeps your body wired rather than tired. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and asks us to bear them patiently. This restless racing may be a contact that touches you and will move on; you might notice one meeting ending and the next one beginning, letting your shoulders drop for just a breath before the next buzz.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield, just after explaining that the self moves through childhood, youth and old age. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings arise and pass away. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them patiently. Your body is caught in a current that has not yet found its edge. The verse points to what moves through you and will move on.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.

verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: With wedding season bringing so many orders, your karigar, supplier, and client are all pressing at once. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go; they do not last, so bear them. You can notice this pressure as something that touches and moves on, rather than a storm that defines your whole day.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These states arise and pass away. They do not last. One should bear them with patience. Your wedding season rush is a contact between your senses and many demands. It brings heat that rises and falls. It does not define who you are.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel your plate is overflowing and you are wound up tight. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go; they do not last, so bear them patiently. This week’s extra demands are contacts that touch you and then move on, leaving space once they pass. Notice the next deadline arriving and leaving without letting it settle in your chest.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna has collapsed in grief on the battlefield. Arjuna fears that if the self never dies, then this crushing sorrow makes no sense. Krishna replies that the senses meet the world and produce cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These sensations arrive and depart on their own. They do not stay. Therefore Arjuna must bear them without letting either joy or grief carry him away. What truly is in a person outlasts every passing ache. Your plate is full and everyone keeps piling more on. The anger you feel is a contact that touched you and is now moving through, not a permanent state that owns you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel the pressure of your first job and that everything is urgent. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last. You can bear this urgency patiently, noticing that it, too, has a beginning and an end.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after the self was described as passing through childhood, youth and old age. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These arrive and depart by nature. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them patiently without being swept away by either joy or grief. The urgency at your first job is a contact between your senses and the world. It has a beginning and an end. You can notice it without letting it swallow you whole.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You run a restaurant in December where every day is chaos and you never get to sit down. Bhasa says the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks, never getting a moment's rest, tangled in a net of reckonings like 'this I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do.' Today, that same loop may be running behind your counter. You might notice, just for a breath, the bird of your mind fainted in that net, and let your shoulders drop for a second before the next order comes.
meaning: In the Yoga Vasishtha, the old friend Bhasa speaks to his childhood companion Vilasa after years of separate austerities. Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found peace. Bhasa answers that he has not. The mind is swept along on endless waves of tasks. It never rests. It is caught in a net of reckonings, repeating what is done, what is doing, and what must still be done. The depths of the mind dance with worry. The bird of the mind faints in that tangle.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are stretched across hospital shifts, your mum’s appointments, and the mortgage renewal this month. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact with the world brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, and that they come and go without lasting. In the midst of this month’s demands, you can notice that each pull, like a passing contact, has its own beginning and end, and you can bear the one in front of you right now.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna reminds him that the self inside never dies and never is born. Then he tells Arjuna that sense contact brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These arrive and depart on their own. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them with patience instead of letting grief or joy carry him away.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: You feel targets climbing while the team shrinks, and you do not know how to keep up. Arjuna tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles and his hair stands on end. When work feels unsafe, your body may be reporting the same honest overwhelm before your mind can catch up. Let that dry mouth or trembling hands simply be what is happening right now, as real as the targets on your desk.
meaning: Arjuna speaks these words to Krishna on the battlefield. He has asked Krishna to place their chariot between the two armies. There he sees teachers, uncles, sons, grandsons and friends standing in the enemy ranks. Overcome by pity and fear of killing kin, Arjuna collapses. He reports that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles and his hair stands on end. The verse proposes that even a strong warrior can be taken over by grief and fear. The teaching begins with this honest breakdown rather than with courage. Your body may be reporting the same honest overwhelm before your mind can catch up to shrinking targets and a thinning team.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You face daily pressure with two years left until retirement and the biggest project of your career on your shoulders. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last; bear them patiently. The demands touching you now will move on in their own time. Let this project be one of those passing contacts, and rest in the knowledge that this season, too, will pass.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These states come and go. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them patiently. The teaching rests on the idea that the self outlasts every passing loss and pain. The pressure you carry at work has its own beginning and end. It does not define the whole of who you are.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You feel the shift in how people treat you now that you have made partner. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. This means the way you carry your new standing is already becoming a model others notice. Let your conduct reflect the groundedness you want around you, beginning with how you walk into the office tomorrow.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has been hesitating about whether to fight. Krishna explains that even those who have nothing left to gain still act for the good of the world. He says that whatever a respected person does, others copy. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. The idea is that people take their cue from those they look up. So anyone with standing is responsible for the standard their conduct sets. Your new standing at the firm already shapes how colleagues treat you. The way you carry this success becomes a model others notice before you speak.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You want to remain the same person who began in a dorm room now that your app has crossed a million downloads. Bhartrihari marvels at a freedom to move at will, food eaten without humiliation, noble company, and learning whose only fruit is calm, asking what generous austerity ripened into such a plain, self-respecting life. Let that same wonder meet you today as you look at the quiet mind that started it all.
meaning: The poet Bhartrihari speaks from his Worship of Shiva. He lists the gifts of a simple life. A person can wander freely, eat without shame, live with noble friends, and study that brings only calm. Even when he looks at the world for a long time, his mind stirs only gently. He does not know what generous austerity ripened into this plain, self-respecting life.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You want your first-year raise and the way your friends now see you not to change who you are. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. Your friends already look to you as the one who has more, so your everyday choices quietly shape how they think success should feel and act. Let your groundedness in this new money be the quiet example they notice.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna to act for the world's welfare. Krishna explains that people imitate those they look up to. A respected person does not need to preach. Others simply copy what that person does. The standard set by a great person becomes the rule the world follows. Even someone fully content needs nothing, yet still acts so the world has a living example to follow. Your friends already look to you as the one who has more. Your everyday choices quietly shape how they think success should feel and act. Let your groundedness in this new money be the quiet example they notice.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
