verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. You have been promoted ahead of schedule and want to lead well while keeping your ego in check. This means your conduct right now quietly sets the benchmark your team will follow, so staying grounded in how you show up matters.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna to act for the world's welfare. Now he explains why even those who have nothing left to gain still keep working. He says that whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. The verse proposes that people imitate the conduct of those they look up. So anyone with standing is responsible for the standard their actions set. Your early promotion means your team is watching how you carry this new weight. Your wish to keep your ego in check is exactly the standard they will copy.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel grateful because your business is booming. The poet wonders at a life of freedom, honest food, good company, and a mind that stays calm: he does not know what kindness earned him this. You can hold that same wonder today, noticing the ordinary dignities already around you, like choosing your own hours and working among capable people.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to the reader from the Worship of Shiva. He has just said that moonlight, poetry and good company lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are, and that the wise leave palaces for the forest. Here he lists the goods of a simple life. He says that freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, and a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long are all rare.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: Success gives you an audience. Your team, your juniors, your younger cousins all take cues from how you carry it. Krishna says the world follows the standard the best people set.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You closed the biggest deal of your career and the bonus changed your life, yet you feel uneasy about how you are becoming. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard you set is the one people follow. Your short temper with junior people and your repeated bank-balance checks set a standard your team is already absorbing. You might pause today to notice one small interaction before it sets the tone for those around you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna to work for the welfare of the world. Now Krishna explains that people do not simply copy what a respected person says. They copy what that person actually does. The standard a great person sets becomes the rule the world follows. Even someone who has no personal need still acts, because others look to him and take their cue from his conduct. Your success has given you standing, and the team around you is already watching how you use it. That makes the unease you feel worth paying attention to, not pushing aside.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one the world follows. Your viral moment gives people a cue for how to carry themselves, so your groundedness today becomes the example they quietly adopt.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna to act for the welfare of the world. Now Krishna explains why even those who have found fulfillment keep working. He says that whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. The wise act not for their own gain but because people look to them and copy their conduct. Your brand’s sudden rise means people are watching how you move now. The standard you set today becomes the quiet cue they adopt.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one people follow. This means your team and those around you are already taking their cue from how you carry this win. Let your groundedness in the moment be the standard they quietly follow.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna to act for the welfare of the world. Now he explains that people do not learn from words alone. They watch what a respected person does and copy it. A great person sets a standard by simply showing up and acting. Others follow that conduct, whether the leader gains anything or not. Your team is already watching how you hold this award and the stage. What you feel right now will quietly shape how they carry success after you leave the room.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You feel determined now that your company has turned a profit for the first time, and you want to think bigger while staying on the ground. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the world follows the standard they set. Your conduct right now quietly shapes how your team and those around you will act, so your grounded next step becomes the example they follow.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while they are on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna to act for the good of the world. Now Krishna explains that people imitate those they look up. Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. The wise keep working even when they have nothing left to gain, because others copy their example. Your first profit means your team is already watching how you move. The way you stay grounded now will quietly become the standard they copy as you grow.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: Your pickle business is now in shops across the state, and you never imagined it. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one people follow. Your humility now sets the tone for everyone watching how success is carried, so let your groundedness be the example they quietly follow.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna to act for the world's welfare. Now he explains that people imitate their leaders. Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. Even someone who is fulfilled and has nothing left to gain keeps working, because if he stopped, the world would follow and fall apart. Your humility now carries weight because others watch how you carry success. It shapes the standard they quietly adopt.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You have been promoted twice in two years, and people now come to you for advice. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard you set is the one people follow. Your rising visibility means your conduct quietly shapes how others handle their own wins and pressure. You can let this awareness remind you to stay steady, so the standard others take from you remains grounded.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just told Arjuna to act for the good of the world. Now Krishna explains that people imitate those they look up. A respected person does something, and others copy it. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. The verse says that even those who are fulfilled keep working. They do not stop because others watch their example and take it as their guide. You have moved fast, and now others look to you before they move. That visibility is real, and it carries weight without asking your permission.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna, listing the qualities that free us and those that bind.
verse_text.line: Show-off, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance: the marks of a nature heading the wrong way.
verse_text.translation: Hypocrisy, arrogance, conceit, anger, harshness and ignorance belong to one born with the demonic nature, Partha.

days.reading: Krishna names these so you can spot them early in yourself: dambha (show), darpa (arrogance), abhimāna (conceit). They grow fastest in a good season.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks how one beyond the three qualities lives; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Even in pain and pleasure, at ease in yourself; earth, stone and gold the same; praise and blame alike.
verse_text.translation: who is the same in pain and pleasure, at home in the self, to whom a clod, a stone and gold are alike, who is the same to the pleasant and the unpleasant, steady, the same in blame and praise,

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to treat a clod of earth, a stone and gold as the same, and to meet praise and blame alike. You are riding a wave of promotion and new respect, yet the fear of your own hype is already here. Let the win land without letting it rewrite who you are; keep your feet on the ground whether the room cheers or stays quiet.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the body as a field, and what true knowledge consists of.
verse_text.line: No need for status, no pretence, no harm, patience, straightness, respect for teachers, purity, steadiness, self-control.
verse_text.translation: Humility, freedom from pretence, non-violence, patience, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadiness and self-control,

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that true knowledge begins with humility and no pretence, followed by patience, uprightness, and self-control. With people now coming to you for advice after your recent promotions, this list gives you ground to stand on: let your steadiness and honesty speak before any hype does. You can hold to these qualities today at work without chasing status.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna sorts knowledge, action, doers, judgement, resolve and happiness by the three qualities.
verse_text.line: Free of clinging and boasting, full of resolve and enthusiasm, unchanged by success or failure: the best kind of doer.
verse_text.translation: The doer who is free from attachment, does not speak of himself, is full of steadiness and enthusiasm, and unmoved by success or failure, is called sattvic.

days.reading: Krishna describes the best kind of doer as full of resolve and enthusiasm, yet free from clinging and boasting, unchanged by success or failure. You are navigating new visibility after two promotions, and this points to bringing steady energy to your work without making the results about your own image. You could pause before your next meeting to remind yourself that the work itself, not the praise, is what matters today.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: The wise see the same self in a scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog and an outcast.
verse_text.translation: The wise see with an equal eye a learned and humble Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and one who eats dog-meat.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that the wise see the same Self in a scholar, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcast. After your two promotions, you could try noticing one colleague today without sizing them up by rank or usefulness. Let that equal eye loosen the pull of your own hype.

story.title: Nahusha's fall
story.summary: King Nahusha was so successful that he was made ruler of heaven. Drunk on it, he made sages carry his palanquin and kicked one to hurry him along. The sage cursed him, and he fell to earth as a giant python. Ages later he seized Bhima in the forest, and was freed only after Yudhishthira answered his questions about what makes a person good.
story.lesson: Success can blind anyone. Conduct is what makes a person good.

days.reading: King Nahusha rose to rule heaven yet grew drunk on power, making sages carry his palanquin until he kicked one and was cursed to become a python. This shows how success can blind anyone, and that conduct is what makes a person good. With people now coming to you for advice, let your own conduct stay steady rather than your standing.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: Nine years in the same job, waking tired and working on autopilot until you crash at night sounds exhausting. Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, looks out his window and says that day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over feels like a mockery to a thinking person. That sense of mockery speaks to your empty feeling today: the repetition itself is absurd, not your worth. Let that absurdity sit with you as you notice the same chain of tasks tomorrow.
meaning: Bali, a king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and looks out at his endless reign. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him about a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind. Bali feels that day after day, night after night, the same chain of tasks returns without end. To a thinking person this repetition feels like a mockery.

verse_text.speaker: Bhasa
verse_text.setting: Two childhood friends meet again in old age; one admits he never found peace.
verse_text.line: 'Done this, doing this, must do that.' Caught in endless lists, the mind never gets a moment's rest.
verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You have been consulting with four days of travel each week for three years, and your body says it is done. The Yoga Vasishtha speaks of a mind carried along on endless waves of tasks, never resting because it is caught in 'done this, doing this, must do that.' Your to-do list may keep running even on a long weekend. Notice that loop, and let your body's signal be the pause to step back and understand what the mind is doing right now.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to Vilasa after they meet again as old men. They grew up together in a forest hermitage, then mourned their fathers and spent years apart in hard austerities. Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found peace. Bhasa answers that he has not. He says the mind is carried along on endless waves of tasks. It never rests because it is caught in the loop of what has been done, what is being done, and what must still be done. The depths of the mind dance with worry. Your body has carried this consulting travel for three years, and the long weekend does not reset it. The verse names the loop that keeps running even when the work stops.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You have spent eight years running your clinic without proper holidays, and you feel like a shell. The Yoga Vasishtha records Bali saying again day, again night, the same chain of tasks over and over, and to a thinking person this feels like a mockery. That sense of being mocked by the repetition can meet you right where you are today, in the quiet after another long shift.
meaning: Bali speaks to himself after ruling the three worlds for ages. He sits by his window and notices that day follows night, and the same tasks return endlessly. He tells himself that to a thinking person, this endless chain feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life becomes a loop, the work itself is not the problem. The task is to master the mind that keeps running the loop. After eight years of running your clinic without proper holidays, the repetition of your days can feel like a trap rather than a life you chose. The verse names that weariness without calling it failure.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'On the Greatness of Time'.
verse_text.line: Same night, same day, the same tasks on repeat. We run in circles and call it living.
verse_text.translation: Thinking 'it is the same night again, the same day', creatures run about in vain, busy as ever with the tasks they have set going; with work full of the same repeated things, tormented by this round of existence, alas, out of delusion we feel no shame.

reading: You dread logging in after only two years because the days have become a loop. Bhartrihari writes that creatures run in circles doing the same tasks, calling it living while time slips away. This verse names that weariness without judging your effort. You might notice one small shift in tomorrow's login that breaks the rerun, even briefly.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks to anyone who reads these lines. He watches creatures rushing through their days. They tell themselves it is the same night again, the same day. They stay busy with tasks they started long ago. Their work is full of repeated things. They are tormented by this round, yet out of delusion they feel no shame. The verse asks us to see that time is passing while we stay busy in circles. You are only two years into your career and the days already feel like a loop. The verse names that weariness without judging the effort you put in.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You have spent three years in short staffing and now feel numb at work and at home. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure is to him, and who he really is beneath it all. When everything you do feels empty, that question can open a real inquiry rather than a dead end. Let the numbness sit with you as you ask who you are beyond the shift.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he looks so low. Rama answers that nothing interests him anymore. He asks what a kingdom or pleasure means to him, who he really is, and what all this is for. He suggests that if it is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as an answer. Your numbness after years of short staffing is a real response to real strain. Rama's question shows that feeling empty can start a genuine inquiry instead of ending in a dead stop.

verse_text.speaker: Vibhishan
verse_text.setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
verse_text.line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
verse_text.translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?

reading: It sounds like home doesn't feel safe right now.

They run about with the same tasks they set going. They are busy as ever, yet tormented by this round. Out of delusion they feel no shame. He speaks to himself about the endless round of days and nights and the same tasks coming again. He feels that this repetition mocks a thinking person. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not more of it but mastering the mind that runs it. Your job is draining you because it keeps asking for the same energy without giving anything back. That loop is real, and it is not your failure.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You are freelancing seven days a week to keep clients happy, and you feel fried and unable to stop. Krishna tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings heat and cold, pleasure and pain, which come and go and do not last, and asks to bear them patiently. This means the pressure you carry right now has a boundary; it moves through you like weather, and you can meet it without letting it define your whole day.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna grieves the coming war. Krishna reminds him that the self inside never dies and never is born. Then he says that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings come and go and do not last. He asks Arjuna to bear them patiently. The pressure to keep clients happy seven days a week moves through you like weather. It has a boundary, and you do not have to let it define your whole day.

verse_text.speaker: Bali

reading: After 35 years of service, you are dragging yourself through the last two with no energy left. Bali, sitting by his window, says again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks, and feels mocked by it. This verse sees that same loop and names the exhaustion without calling it meaningless. You might rest in the simple fact that the repetition is seen, not dismissed.
meaning: The demon king Bali, who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and watches the same days and nights repeat. He remembers a riddle his father Virochana once told him about a silent king and a powerful minister. The minister is the mind. Bali feels mocked by the endless chain of the same tasks, and this disenchantment opens his search for an aim that leaves nothing further to do. After thirty-five years of service, the last two feel like the same chain repeating without end. The verse names that loop and sees the exhaustion without calling it meaningless.

verse_text.speaker: Bali

verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: Six days on site, then room, then site again—your body is tired in a way rest does not touch. Bali, sitting by his window, says again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks, and feels mocked by it. That same loop might echo in your weeks, not as proof your work is worthless, but as a sign that your mind is awake to the repetition. You could let that noticing point toward one small shift today, perhaps a different route back to your room.
meaning: Bali, a king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and wonders what his life adds up to. He sees the same days and nights, the same duties rising and falling like waves, and he tells himself that to a thinking person this endless round feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the way forward is not to abandon the work but to master the mind that runs it.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna, seeing his own family in the enemy ranks, collapses in grief before the battle.
verse_text.line: Shaking limbs, a dry mouth, a racing body: the Gita opens with a panic attack, not a hero.
verse_text.translation: My limbs give way, my mouth is parched, my body trembles and my hair stands on end.

reading: You are facing a 60-day window after your company announced restructuring. Arjuna tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end. This verse names the same physical overwhelm you may feel right now, showing that panic can take the body before any answer arrives.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield of after Krishna has driven the chariot between the two armies. Arjuna sees his teachers, uncles, sons, grandsons and friends standing on the enemy side. He collapses in grief and fear. He tells Krishna that his limbs give way, his mouth is parched, his body trembles and his hair stands on end. The verse proposes that even a strong warrior can be taken over by his body before he finds any answer. It begins the Gita with a breakdown, not a hero. You are facing a sixty day window after your company announced restructuring. Arjuna names the same physical overwhelm you may feel right now, showing that panic can take the body before any answer arrives.

reading: With payment stuck in the market and your supplier calling every day while the shop rent is still due, you are carrying a heavy load. meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna has driven the chariot between the two armies. Arjuna sees his own teachers, uncles, sons, grandsons and friends standing in the enemy ranks. It shows that even a strong warrior can freeze when what he loves is threatened. Your body is carrying the same strain that Arjuna named, under the weight of stuck payments and daily calls.

The verse proposes that even the strongest people can freeze in the face of overwhelming loss. Your body is registering the shock of redundancy just as Arjuna's registered the sight of his family. The uncertainty you feel has a physical shape.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: A year of monthly losses has brought your savings to the edge, and right now you feel stuck. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna put down his bow and sank onto his chariot seat, his mind overwhelmed by grief. In the same way, this verse names the moment of laying everything down when you simply cannot go on. It points to the very spot where the teaching begins, not to the end of the road.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra on the battlefield. Arjuna has just argued that he would rather die unarmed than kill his own kin. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna then puts down his bow and arrows and sinks onto the chariot seat, his mind overwhelmed by grief. The verse names a moment of total collapse where grief has taken away the will to act.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna calls these mātrā-sparśa: contacts, things that touch you and move on. A deadline, a bad week, a hard meeting. They hurt while they last, they pass, and Krishna asks you to bear them (titikṣasva) until they do.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Without inner discipline there's no clarity; without clarity, no peace; and without peace, where is happiness?
verse_text.translation: For the undisciplined there is no understanding and no steady contemplation. Without contemplation there is no peace, and for the one without peace, where is happiness?

days.reading: Krishna lays out a chain. An unsettled mind has no clarity, without clarity there is no peace, and without peace there is no happiness, however good things look on paper. The workload is one part of stress. The other part is a mind with no place to stand.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on working in the world without being stained by it.
verse_text.line: Like a lotus leaf in water, do your work without letting the mess soak in.
verse_text.translation: One who acts offering all actions to the Supreme, giving up attachment, is not touched by wrong, as a lotus leaf is not wet by water.

days.reading: A lotus leaf sits in water all its life, and the water still beads and rolls off it. Krishna uses it for someone who works fully and lets the mess around them roll off. You stay in the pond and keep your surface dry.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Rivers pour into the ocean and it stays full and still. Let desires enter you the same way.
verse_text.translation: As waters enter the ocean, which is ever being filled yet stays unmoved within its shores, so the one into whom all desires enter in the same way finds peace, not the one who craves desires.

days.reading: Rivers keep pouring into the ocean and it stays full and still. Demands will keep coming. In Krishna's picture, peace comes from being deep enough to take them in.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Moderate in food and rest, in work and play, in sleep and waking: that's how sorrow eases.
verse_text.translation: For one who is moderate in food and recreation, measured in effort at work, moderate in sleep and waking, yoga becomes the destroyer of sorrow.

days.reading: This is the Gita at its most practical. Krishna tells Arjuna that the yoga which ends sorrow belongs to someone moderate in food, movement, work, sleep and waking. A lot of stress starts as a schedule with no rest built into it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on acting free of ego, like and dislike, in your own way.
verse_text.line: Hand your work to something higher, drop the 'mine' and the hoping, and act with the fever gone.
verse_text.translation: Surrendering all actions to me, with your mind on the inner self, free from hope and the sense of 'mine', fight with your fever gone.

days.reading: The Sanskrit is vigata-jvaraḥ: with the fever gone. Krishna still wants Arjuna to fight, and to fight without the heat of 'mine' and anxious hoping. Offer the work to something larger than your worry, and do it.

story.title: Janaka on the palace roof
story.summary: Walking in his garden one spring, King Janaka overheard hidden sages singing about the self. Shaken, he climbed to his palace roof and questioned everything he had lived for. When his attendant came to call him to the day's work, he could have walked away from the throne. He didn't. He went back and did his duties, but with a mind that no longer clutched.
story.lesson: You don't have to leave your life to change it. Do the day's work with a mind that doesn't clutch.

days.reading: When stress builds, it's tempting to dream of quitting everything. Janaka kept the same work and held it differently.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From the section on the wicked: the impossible position of anyone who serves a master.
verse_text.line: Quiet, you're dull; talkative, a show-off; patient, weak. Serving a boss is harder than yoga.
verse_text.translation: Keep quiet and you are dumb; speak well and you are a babbler or a windbag; stay close and you are pushy; keep away and you lack confidence; be patient and you are a coward; refuse to put up with things and you are ill-bred. The duty of serving another is deep indeed, beyond the reach even of yogis.

reading: Your boss tore up your report in front of everyone, calling it nonsense. Bhartrihari writes that serving a master means every silence is dullness and every word is a show; be patient and you are weak, refuse and you are ill-bred. This verse names a trap where any choice gets twisted into a fault, so you can stop hunting for the one perfect reply and simply hold to your own standard for the work you did.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this to the reader from the section on wicked people. He describes the impossible position of anyone who serves a master. No matter what a person does, it gets twisted into a fault. Stay quiet and you are dull. Speak well and you are a show-off. Be patient and you are weak. Refuse and you are ill-bred. Serving another is a duty so deep that even yogis cannot fathom it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on duties by nature and finding fulfilment in your own work.
verse_text.line: Better your own path, imperfectly walked, than someone else's done perfectly.
verse_text.translation: Better is one's own duty, though imperfect, than the duty of another well performed. Doing the work born of one's own nature, one incurs no wrong.

reading: A younger man from outside was hired for the permanent role, and you have been acting head for two years. Krishna says it is better to walk your own path, even imperfectly, than to perform another's duty well. Your two years of leading carry their own weight, separate from the title that was given to someone else.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield after listing duties tied to social station. He tells Arjuna that perfection comes from doing one's own work as an offering. One's own path, even when flawed, beats another's path done perfectly. Acting in line with one's own nature brings no fault. Your two years of leading carry their own weight, separate from the title that was given to someone else.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Censure of Craving': the poet to his own hope.
verse_text.line: I swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. Hope, how much longer will you make me dance?
verse_text.translation: I somehow put up with the taunts of the wicked while trying to please them; I held back my tears and laughed with an empty heart; I folded my hands even before people whose minds were numbed by money. Hope, futile hope, how much more will you make me dance?

reading: You worked ten years and the promotion went to someone else, leaving you feeling unseen. Bhartrihari cries out to Hope, saying he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart, asking how much longer Hope will make him dance. Today, your own long effort can feel like that forced laughter, empty and unnoticed.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to his own hope from the section Censure of Craving. He has spent his life digging for treasure, flattering kings and enduring shabby treatment. He tells hope that he swallowed insults and forced laughter with an empty heart. He asks how much longer hope will make him dance like this. You gave ten years and the reward went elsewhere, so the effort now feels hollow and unseen.

The point is to do the work that fits you, with all its flaws, as an offering. Your own effort carries worth even when it feels overlooked. It matters more than measuring your path against the polished progress of others.

Your manager talks over you in meetings and then calls you quiet in reviews. The verse shows that the fault is in the position, not in you.

verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: 'My Plan of Campaign', Madras, February 1897, on friends who turned critics.
verse_text.line: as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.
verse_text.translation: We hear so much tall talk in this world, of liberal ideas and sympathy with differences of opinion. That is very good, but as a fact, we find that one sympathises with another only so long as the other believes in everything he has to say, but as soon as he dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes.

reading: You feel the sting of having your part erased in front of others. Swami Vivekananda observed that sympathy often vanishes the moment someone dares to differ. Your co-founder taking the investor credit alone shows how quickly support can disappear when you do not align. You can notice this shift without deciding you were wrong to stand apart.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda spoke these words to an audience at Victoria Hall in Madras in February eighteen ninety seven. He had recently returned from the and was facing critics who claimed others had made his success. He told the crowd that people often praise liberal ideas and sympathy for differing views. Yet in practice, they support one another only while agreement lasts. The moment someone dares to differ, that sympathy is gone, that love vanishes. Your co-founder took the investor credit alone while you stood beside him. This verse names the sudden disappearance of support when you do not align, without saying you were wrong to stand apart.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: You carry the ache of words that cut deepest when they come from those closest to you. Krishna speaks of his heart churning like fire being rubbed from a stick, saying even relatives' harsh words keep burning him day after day. That same fire can live in you too, long after the moment has passed. You might let that burning remind you that your pain is real, not imagined.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds within his own clan. He tells Narada that he gives his relatives half of what he owns and bears their harsh words, yet his heart still churns like fire being rubbed from a stick. The harsh words his kin speak keep burning him, day after day. Your father's speech at your wedding left a mark that still sits with you, because the words came from the people who were meant to hold you up.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You feel alone when your husband’s family only reaches out for their own needs and your husband does not defend you. Krishna tells Arjuna, see me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. In the midst of this hurt, the verse names a bond that no distance or silence can break: you are never out of sight. You can rest in that steadiness today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just described the person who sees the self in all beings and all beings in the self. Now he restates this in his own voice. He says that whoever sees him everywhere and sees everything resting in him will never be lost to him, and he will never be lost to that person. The idea is that a settled mind rests in this mutual seeing, and it returns gently again and again. You are carrying a hurt that no spiritual idea can erase. Yet the verse offers a steadiness that stays even when human voices fall silent.

That inner breaking you feel is real and named. Let this truth sit with you: even the divine feels that burn, and your pain is not imagined.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing weary of feuds within his own clan. He describes how the harsh words his relatives speak continue to burn his heart like a fire-stick being rubbed. The verse proposes that in family conflict, the only effective weapon is not force but gentleness, patience and respect. Krishna names the same slow burn you carry after those words reached you. The fracture you feel inside has a name, and it is not yours to carry alone.

Krishna speaks of harsh words from relatives that keep burning him, day after day. Let those burning words sit with you as Krishna named his own, without deciding what your siblings truly meant.

He tells Narada that he gives his relatives half of what he owns and bears their harsh words, yet those words still grind his heart like a fire-stick being churned for flame. Your siblings have turned your sacrifice into a story about greed, and that misreading cuts because it denies the care you gave.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You have spent fifteen years sending money home, and now your brother claims you did nothing for the family. Ram says the deepest sorrow is not the loss itself, but that the one he loved did not face him and tell him directly. Your brother’s words may burn because they came without that honest facing, not merely because of the money.
meaning: Rama has just accepted fourteen years in the forest. Kaikeyi has told him that Bharata must be crowned instead. He agrees at once and shows no anger. Yet one thing still wounds him. He speaks to Kaikeyi about his father. He says only the king not telling him this himself burns his heart. The loss is large, but the real pain is the absence of a direct word from the one he loved. Your brother twists what you gave into nothing. The verse shows that the wound is not only the money lost, but that he did not meet you and say it straight.

meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing tired of feuds inside his own clan. He tells Narada that even he feels the sting of his relatives' harsh words. He says his heart is churned like a fire-stick being rubbed to spark flame. The words keep burning him day after day. The point is that in family conflict the only working weapon is gentleness, patience and respect.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has lain on the shore for three days asking the ocean for a way across. No answer comes.
verse_text.line: Calm, patience, honesty and kind words: people who don't value them will read them as weakness.
verse_text.translation: See the ocean's arrogance: he does not even show himself. Calm, forbearance, straightforwardness and gentle speech, these virtues of the good, are taken by the unworthy as signs of weakness.

days.reading: Ram tells Lakshman that the ocean's silence shows arrogance: calm, patience, honesty and gentle speech are read as weakness by those who lack them. Your hurt from mummy's harsh words fits here, because your kindness is being read as something small rather than strength. The verse sees the misreading coming from the other person's lack, not from any flaw in you.

verse_text.ref: Mahabharata · Vana Parva · Vana: Draupadi and Yudhishthira
verse_text.speaker: Prahlada (quoted by Draupadi)
verse_text.setting: Draupadi quotes old Prahlada answering his grandson: is forgiveness better, or force?
verse_text.line: Force isn't always right, and forgiveness isn't always right. Wisdom is knowing which the moment needs.
verse_text.translation: Force is not always best, and forgiveness is not always best. Know this for certain, my child: both have their place.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Uttanka, furious that the war happened, threatens to curse Krishna for not stopping it.
verse_text.line: I tried hard to make peace. When people refuse to be reconciled, you can't force it.
verse_text.translation: I made every effort earlier to bring the Kauravas to peace. But they could not be brought to agree, however I tried.

days.reading: Krishna tells the sage Uttanka that he tried hard to bring the Kauravas to peace, yet they refused to agree no matter how he tried. You do not have to carry the weight of fixing this alone when harsh words keep burning. Stand on the ground that you made every honest effort, and the rest is not yours to force.

verse_text.speaker: Seer
verse_text.setting: The creation story: last of all, dharma is made.
verse_text.line: Nothing is higher than what is right. With it the weak can face the strong. What is right is truth.
verse_text.translation: Still he did not flourish. So he created a higher form, dharma. Dharma is the power over power; nothing is higher than dharma. Through dharma even a weak man can stand up to a strong one, as with the help of a king. That dharma is truth. So people say of one who speaks truth, 'He speaks dharma,' and of one who speaks dharma, 'He speaks truth.' Both are the same.

days.reading: The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad says that nothing is higher than what is right, and through it the weak can face the strong. You could state one true fact about your studies today, letting what is right stand between you and the harsh words. This truth is not about winning quickly, but about anchoring yourself in what is fair.

verse_text.speaker: Kabandha
verse_text.setting: Ram is lost and grieving; Kabandha tells him to seek Sugriva, who has also lost his wife and home.
verse_text.line: Find a friend who knows your kind of trouble. You won't get through this alone.
verse_text.translation: You must make him your friend, best of friends. Thinking it over, I see no success for you without it.

days.reading: Kabandha tells Ram, who is lost and grieving, to seek Sugriva as a friend because he also lost his wife and home. You could reach out to one person who has faced a similar hurt today. Shared trouble can open a door that isolation keeps closed.

story.title: Hanuman finds a friend in Lanka
story.summary: Searching Lanka, Hanuman is surprised to find a house with Ram's name on it. Its owner, Vibhishan, Ravana's brother, says he lives in Lanka like a tongue among teeth. Hanuman tells him even a restless monkey like himself was given Ram's love.
story.lesson: Even in a hostile place there may be one ally; find them.

days.reading: In the Sundar Kand, Hanuman finds Ravana’s brother Vibhishan living inside Lanka like a tongue among teeth, unable to share his values with those around him. Vibhishan calls himself lowly and without practice, yet speaking with Hanuman brings him a rest beyond words. You, too, carry hurt from words that keep burning, and this scene shows how one true meeting with someone who knows your kind of trouble can bring rest even before anything changes around you.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You feel like a stranger in your own home because your mother-in-law criticises your parenting and your husband dismisses you. Ram says the deepest sorrow is not the loss itself, but that the one he loved did not face him and tell him directly. The hurt you carry today may be that the people closest to you have not met you with honest words, leaving you alone with the weight of their silence.
meaning: Rama speaks to Kaikeyi after she has demanded his exile and Bharata's coronation. He accepts the fourteen years in the forest without anger. Yet one thing still burns in him. He says the king did not tell him the news himself. The verse proposes that a person can bear the loss itself. What wounds is the absence of a direct, honest word from the one they love.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: You feel lost after being betrayed by your own family. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna, the greatest archer, put down his bow and sat in his chariot, his mind overwhelmed by grief. This verse names the moment when everything feels too heavy to carry. It speaks to you today as the place where you can lay down what you are holding, exactly as Arjuna did.
meaning: Sanjaya speaks to the blind king Dhritarashtra from the battlefield. Arjuna has just argued that killing his own kin is worse than death. He says he would rather be killed unarmed. Sanjaya reports that Arjuna then puts down his bow and arrows. He sinks onto the chariot seat, his mind overwhelmed by grief. The verse names the moment when even the strongest person freezes and can no longer act. You are in that same frozen moment after your family turned on you. The verse shows that collapse can come before any answer, and it does not rush you past it.

verse_text.ref: Complete Works, Vol. 5, Epistles – First Series, CIII, p. 160
verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: Letter from Belur, 18 May 1901, ill and grieving the sudden death of the Raja of Khetri.
verse_text.line: Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.
verse_text.translation: The Raja of Khetri died from a fall a few months ago. So you see things are all gloomy with me just now, and my own health is wretched. Yet I am sure to bob up soon and am waiting for the next turn.

days.reading: Swami Vivekananda wrote that his own health is wretched and things are gloomy right now, yet he is sure to bob up soon and is simply waiting for the next turn. This speaks to the low patch after loss you are in: it names the darkness plainly without pretending it is gone. You can sit with the gloom today and still decide to wait for the next turn, without deciding when it will arrive.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what becomes of someone who tries and fails; Krishna reassures him.
verse_text.line: Whoever does good never comes to ruin, my friend. Not here, not after.
verse_text.translation: The Blessed Lord said: Partha, there is no ruin for him either in this world or the next. No one who does good, my friend, ever comes to grief.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever does good never comes to ruin, here or after. Even when you have been betrayed by your own family and hope feels thin, the good you have tried to do is not wasted. Your effort carries forward, so you can stand on what remains.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on worship for rewards and worship without desire.
verse_text.line: Turn to me with your whole heart, and I will carry what you lack and guard what you have.
verse_text.translation: To those who think of me alone and worship me, ever devoted, I bring what they lack and preserve what they have.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever turns to him with their whole heart, he will carry what they lack and guard what they have. After the weight of betrayal by your own family, this invites you to stop holding everything together alone. You still take the next practical step, while trusting that what is missing is being carried and what remains is being guarded.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna to lift himself by his own self and not let himself sink, for the self alone is the friend of the self and the enemy of the self. When hope feels low after being betrayed by your own family, the harshest voice can be your own. You could notice one thought today that pushes you down, and replace it with the gentler words you would offer a friend. Asking for help is part of being on your own side, just as Arjuna does.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: Yoga is unhooking from sorrow. Practise it with resolve and a heart that doesn't lose hope.
verse_text.translation: Know that to be yoga: the breaking of contact with sorrow. This yoga should be practised with determination and with an undespairing mind.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that yoga is unhooking from sorrow, and to practise it with resolve and a heart that doesn't lose hope. You could sit with this for a few minutes today, letting the practice be simply about loosening sorrow's grip a little, not fixing everything at once. This builds on the steadiness you began on Day 3.

story.title: Ram waits out the monsoon
story.summary: After Sita was taken, the rains came, and Ram had to wait four months on a mountainside before any search could begin. Nothing could be done. He couldn't sleep for grief. Lakshman sat with him and reminded him that endless grieving drains every purpose, and that this was a season for waiting, not for giving up. Ram resolved to wait well, and when the rains ended, the search began.
story.lesson: Some seasons are for waiting. Wait well, without letting grief take you.

days.reading: After Sita was taken, Ram had to wait four months on a mountainside while the rains blocked every search; he could not sleep for grief, yet Lakshman reminded him that endless grieving drains purpose, so this was a season for waiting. You, feeling lost after being betrayed by your own family, are in a season where action is blocked. Wait well on your mountainside without letting grief take you, and let the search begin when the rains end.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You trusted a friend with your business and were stabbed in the back. Krishna tells Arjuna that when a person dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, which blocked turns into anger. This verse speaks to the fire that builds after trust is broken, showing how the mind keeps returning to what was lost. Notice where your thoughts rest after the betrayal, and let that awareness sit with the wound you carry today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna has just asked what a person of steady wisdom looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna answers by tracing a chain inside the mind. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and from desire, when it is blocked, comes anger. The verse proposes that steadiness is built by guarding where attention rests, because anger begins with what the mind keeps turning over. The betrayal by your business partner has left a raw wound, and the anger you feel is real. This verse names how the mind feeds that fire by returning again and again to what was lost.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You have carried a silence for two years after your daughter stopped speaking to you. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else can truly know this ache; only the heart knows the love it misses. Your loneliness may hold a grief that words only touch lightly, and that private ache belongs to your own heart alone.
meaning: In the Sundar Kand of the Ramcharitmanas, Ram sends a message to Sita through Hanuman. Sita is captive and has nearly lost hope. Hanuman has already told her Ram's story and dropped Ram's ring from a tree. Now Ram says that speaking of pain lightens it a little. But whom can he tell, since no one else knows this ache. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them. Your daughter's silence has left you with a grief that words only touch lightly, and no one else can carry the weight of what you miss.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: You feel hurt because your parents take your brother's side and act like you are being dramatic. In the Ramayana, Ram says the one sorrow burning his heart is not the news itself, but that the person he loved did not face him and tell him directly. This speaks to you today by naming the sting of being sidelined rather than confronted, and by showing that the way a truth reaches us can wound as deeply as the truth itself.
meaning: In the Ayodhya Kanda of the Valmiki Ramayana, Ram has just agreed to fourteen years of exile after Kaikeyi demands it. He shows no anger and accepts the loss at once. Yet he tells Kaikeyi that only one sorrow burns his heart. It is not the news of the coronation or the exile. It is that his father, the king, did not tell him himself. The verse proposes that a person can accept a hard outcome. What wounds is that the one they love did not walk out and face them directly.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (quoted by Bhishma)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, tired of feuds in his own clan, confides in the sage Narada and asks how to keep the peace.
verse_text.line: Harsh words from family can keep burning long after they're said. Even Krishna felt it.
verse_text.translation: My heart is churned the way someone wanting fire churns a fire-stick. The harsh words my relatives say keep burning me, day after day.

reading: At a wedding, your elder brother humiliated you while everyone laughed along. Bhishma records Krishna saying that harsh words from relatives keep burning day after day, churning the heart like fire-sticks. That lingering heat after public mockery is real, and the verse names it plainly without asking you to absorb it.
meaning: Krishna speaks to the sage Narada after growing tired of feuds inside his own clan. He admits that even he feels ground down by the harsh words his relatives speak. He says his heart is churned like a fire-stick being rubbed to make flame. The words keep burning him, day after day. The verse proposes that in family conflict the only effective weapon is gentleness, patience and respect. Your brother's words at the wedding still carry heat because they came from blood and were witnessed by others. The verse names that exact burn without asking you to carry it alone.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: After sharing your first real breakup with me, you are carrying a heavy ache. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet no one else truly knows this hurt; only the heart alone knows the love it misses. Your loneliness right now may feel like a secret only you hold, and naming it aloud, even just here, can carry a little of that weight.
meaning: Ram speaks this to Sita through Hanuman. Sita sits captive in the grove after Ravana takes her. Hanuman has just dropped Ram's ring from a tree and told her Ram's whole story. Now Ram's message reaches her across the sea. He says that telling grief lightens it a little. But he asks whom he can tell, since no one else knows this pain. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them. Your first real breakup has left you with a grief no one around you can fully map. Naming the ache here can carry a little of its weight.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You are living through a house that echoes now that your husband has moved out. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet whom can he tell, for no one else knows this ache. The love your heart holds knows its own weight. Let the quiet rooms carry what your voice alone can name today.
meaning: Ram speaks these words to Sita through Hanuman. Sita sits captive in the grove after Ravana threatens her. Hanuman has just dropped Ram's ring to her and told her Ram's story. Ram says that telling grief eases it a little, but there is no one to tell, for no one else knows this pain. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them. Your husband has moved out and the weekends leave the house empty. Ram's words meet that exact hollow, the sense that the ache has no witness.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: Hanuman speaks to Sita that telling grief lightens it a little, yet no one else truly knows this ache. You, in a now-empty home after twenty years of marriage, may find that speaking brings only a small relief, because this loneliness is deeply your own. The heart alone holds what it misses, and that private knowing stays with you today.
meaning: Ram speaks this to Sita through Hanuman in the grove. Sita is captive after Ravana took her, and Hanuman has just told her Ram's whole story. Ram says that speaking of pain lightens it a little. But he asks whom he can tell, because no one else knows this ache. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them. The verse proposes that naming grief offers a small relief, yet some sorrow stays hidden because no listener truly shares it. After twenty years of marriage, the silence in your home carries a weight only you fully know. Speaking about the emptiness may ease it slightly, but the depth of what you miss remains a private truth that stays with you.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You described nine years in the same bed as different worlds, with no fights left. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet asks whom he can tell, since no one knows this ache. Your heart alone knows the love you miss in that quiet distance. Let that private knowing sit with you today as you share the same room.
meaning: Ram speaks to Sita through Hanuman while she is held captive. Hanuman has just told Sita Ram's story and dropped his ring. Sita has nearly lost hope. Ram says that telling grief eases it a little, but he has no one to tell, because only his own heart knows the truth of their love and the depth of this pain. He is saying that some sorrow is so private that words cannot fully carry it, yet the act of speaking still offers a small relief. In your nine years of sharing a bed without a shared world, that private ache belongs to you alone. The distance you feel is real, and only your heart knows what it misses.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.

verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

meaning: Ram speaks these words to Sita through Hanuman. Sita sits captive, threatened by Ravana, and has nearly lost hope. But Ram asks whom he can tell, since no one else knows this pain. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between him and Sita.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: Your wife has taken the children to India and says she will not return. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet whom can he tell, since no one else knows this ache. The truth of the love you shared knows only your own heart. That private weight belongs to you alone right now.
meaning: Ram speaks to Sita through Hanuman while she is held captive. She has nearly lost hope after their long separation. Ram says that telling someone about grief eases it a little. Yet he asks whom he can tell, because no one else knows this particular pain. Only his own heart truly knows the depth of the love he misses in her. You are carrying a grief that no one around you can fully enter. The ache of her leaving and the children going with her is yours alone to hold right now.

verse_text.speaker: the gopis
verse_text.setting: The women of Braj, after Krishna has left, on missing him.
verse_text.line: "Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes."
verse_text.translation: Night and day our eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for us.

reading: Missing someone can feel like weather that does not lift. The gopis say that since Shyam went away, it has been monsoon in their eyes, night and day their eyes keep raining. You do not have to fix this ache; you can simply let it be the season you are in right now.
meaning: In the Bhramargeet, the women of Braj speak these lines after Krishna has left. They tell a friend that since Shyam went away, their eyes keep raining night and day. They say it is always the rainy season for them. The verse proposes that weeping for someone you miss can become a whole season rather than a single event. It treats such longing as a form of love itself, not something that must be fixed. Your missing your ex has become a weather you live inside, not a storm that passes in an hour. The verse sees that ache as love still present, not a problem to solve right now.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You are searching the last few years for the moment love slipped away, and the mind keeps turning that search over without finding it. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. Today, that loop of looking back is simply the wind moving; you can notice the searching without forcing it to stop.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the steady yogi who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last because the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that the mind is difficult to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it. Your mind is turning the last few years over and over, looking for the moment love slipped away, and finding nothing. The verse names this restlessness as something hard to hold, not a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.
verse_text.line: Speaking of pain lightens it. But whom can I tell? No one knows this ache.
verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: You carry a hurt from a bond that lasted three years, ended by a single phrase and a block. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet asks whom he can tell, because no one else knows this ache. Your own heart alone holds the truth of what you lost. Let that private knowing sit with you today, without anyone else needing to understand it.
meaning: Ram speaks to Sita while Hanuman carries the message across the sea. Sita sits captive in the grove, threatened by Ravana, and has nearly lost hope. Hanuman has just told her Ram's story and dropped his ring to her. Ram says that speaking of pain lightens it a little, but asks whom he can tell, because no one else knows this ache. Only his own heart knows the truth of the love between them.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram's message to Sita, carried across the sea by Hanuman.

verse_text.translation: Telling one's grief lightens it a little. But whom can I tell? No one knows this pain. The truth of the love between you and me, my beloved, only my own heart knows.

reading: Today the papers are signed. Ram tells Sita that speaking of pain lightens it a little, yet asks whom he can tell, since no one else knows this ache. You might carry a grief that no one around you can fully share. Let the truth of what you miss rest, for now, in your own heart alone.
meaning: Ram sends this message to Sita through Hanuman. She is held captive in the grove, threatened by Ravana, and has nearly lost hope. Only the guard Trijata has shown her kindness. Hanuman has already dropped Ram's ring to her and told her Ram's whole story. Now Ram speaks through Hanuman. He says that telling one's grief lightens it a little. But then he asks whom he can tell, since no one else knows this pain. He adds that only his own heart knows the truth of the love between him and Sita. You signed the papers today. The grief you carry may be too private for the people around you to fully enter. Let that truth rest in your own heart for now.

verse_text.speaker: the gopis
verse_text.setting: The women of Braj, after Krishna has left, on missing him.
verse_text.line: "Since he left, it has been monsoon in our eyes."
verse_text.translation: Night and day our eyes keep raining. Ever since Shyam went away, it is always the rainy season for us.

reading: Since he left, your eyes have kept raining night and day. Ever since he went away, it has been monsoon there. Your daughter still asks when he is coming home, and that waiting can feel like weather that does not lift.
meaning: The gopis, the cowherd women of Braj, speak these words to a friend after Krishna has gone. They tell her that ever since Shyam left, their eyes have kept raining night and day. The verse says that weeping for someone you miss is allowed. The loss is so total that tears become a season instead of a single event. Your eyes have kept raining since he left. Your daughter still asks when papa is coming home, and that waiting can feel like weather that does not lift.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: Your marriage went cold once the kids grew up, and he is there, but not with you. Krishna tells Arjuna, See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me. In this quiet distance, that same steadiness can meet you: the bond you share is not erased by the space between you two. You might rest your attention on one ordinary thing today—a cup, a breath—and let that be the place where you are still held.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching him how to settle the mind through meditation. He tells Arjuna that a person who sees the divine everywhere and sees all things resting within the divine will never be separated from it, and the divine will never lose sight of that person. The verse proposes that this steady seeing brings a bond that distance cannot break.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna (message to Yashoda)
verse_text.setting: Krishna, far from home in Mathura, sends a message to his mother.
verse_text.line: "Since I left you, no one has called me by my pet name."
verse_text.translation: Stay well, mother Yashoda. In four or five days we two brothers will come. Since the day I was parted from you, no one has called me "Kanhaiya". I have not had breakfast in the morning, nor warm milk at evening.

reading: You are 8000 miles away while your mom lives alone in Indore and had a dizzy spell. Krishna, far from home, tells his mother that since he left, no one has called him by his pet name or shared his morning breakfast and evening warm milk with him. This shows that the ache of distance is not only yours; he too misses the ordinary tenderness of being known at home. You might hold onto the thought that she too feels the weight of this separation, even across the miles.
meaning: Krishna sends a message through to his foster mother Yashoda. He is far from home in Mathura after killing. He tells her to stay well and that he and his brother will come in four or five days. He adds that since the day he left her, no one has called him by his pet name Kanhaiya, and he has not had his morning breakfast or his evening warm milk. The verse proposes that missing home is love. It shows that the one who leaves also longs for the ordinary tenderness of home. Your mother feels the weight of this distance too, even while she stays in her own home.

You might hold onto the thought of their voices calling you by your childhood name.

You wake at night to check your mother's breathing, and this verse speaks to that quiet ache of missing the ordinary tenderness only home holds. You might send her a message that you are well, and that you miss being known by your home name.

He adds that since he left home, no one there calls him Kanhaiya. He has missed his morning breakfast and his evening warm milk. The verse shows that love in separation goes both ways. The prince misses the ordinary tenderness of home, a pet name and a mother's food. Your watch at night comes from the same love that moves Krishna. You miss the ordinary tenderness only home holds, not grand gestures.

Like him, you may feel the absence most in small, tender things—a home name, a familiar meal—rather than in grand gestures, and that quiet missing is real.
