Your missing shows up in small tender things like a home name or a familiar meal, and that quiet absence is real.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: Arjuna asks this, and many of us ask it too: what pushes a person to do wrong, even unwillingly, as if forced? If you're carrying something you did, you've probably asked it at night. The Gita treats the question as worth a full answer.
meaning: Arjuna, the warrior on the battlefield, asks Krishna why a person does wrong even against their own will, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger, and this desire is the enemy that clouds a person's wisdom like smoke over a fire. The verse proposes that a person can master this force only by seeing it clearly for what it is.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Your days hold mummy’s dialysis three times a week and small children, and a fear rises every day. Krishna hears Arjuna say the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. In your quiet moments, that same wind can feel like it is blowing through the house; you do not have to catch it. Let it move, and notice one breath that is still yours.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi as one who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such steady evenness cannot last, because the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, as hard to hold as the wind. Krishna answers that practice and letting go can train it. Your mind is not failing because it races between your mother's dialysis and your children. It is simply doing what minds do when they carry too much at once.

days.reading: Yudhishthira tells Draupadi not to answer anger with anger. The one who stays calm protects both people and heals both. days.reading: The Aitareya Upanishad says the one who nourishes the child must herself be nourished. story.title: A poor widow's small son is afraid to walk home through the woods
story.summary: Gopala's mother is a widow, very poor, who has toiled at her spinning wheel for months to buy his school things. One winter afternoon he tells her he is afraid to walk home alone through the dark woods; other boys have someone to fetch them. 'Never before had she felt her widowhood, her loneliness, her poverty so bitter.'
story.lesson: A parent's faith, passed to a child, makes the child unafraid; love and faith, more than learning, bring the Lord near.

days.reading: Swami Vivekananda retold a devotional tale of a poor widow whose son fears walking home through dark woods. She remembers that the Lord carries what is needed for those who depend on him, wipes her tears, and tells her boy to call his brother Gopala in the trees. Your overthinking meets a parent's loneliness here: you can pass trust to your daughter even when words are slow, letting faith stand beside her silence.

verse_text.translation: Carried along on endless great waves of tasks, the mind never gets a moment's rest; its depths dance with worry. 'This I've done, this I'm doing, this I'll do': so the bird of the mind, tangled in a net of reckonings, faints.

reading: You carry lists that stay uncrossed by Wednesday, and the weight of it leaves you feeling like garbage. The Yoga Vasishtha describes a mind swept along by endless waves of tasks, caught in 'done, doing, must do,' and fainting under that net. Today, that same loop might be showing you where rest is being asked for, not through a harder push, but through stepping back to see what the mind is actually doing.
meaning: Bhasa speaks to his old friend Vilasa, whom they meet again as old men after years apart. Vilasa asks if Bhasa has found peace. Bhasa answers that there is none while the mind keeps spinning through endless tasks. He says the mind is carried along on great waves of to-do lists, never resting, its depths dancing with worry. The reckoning of what is done, what is doing, and what must still be done tangles the bird of the mind in a net, and it faints. Your Sunday lists carry the same endless waves Bhasa describes, and the uncrossed items by Wednesday leave you feeling like garbage rather than simply tired.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse_text.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: You feel stuck in procrastination. Rama tells the sages that the mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy. This is an ordinary pattern of the untrained mind, not a flaw in you. When you sit down to begin, you might notice the same swooping and losing interest, and simply naming that movement is a concrete first step.
meaning: Rama speaks to the sages Vishvamitra and Vasishtha after they ask why he has grown so withdrawn. He is describing his restless mind. He says the mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy. He is naming the problem honestly. The verse proposes that seeing this empty pattern clearly is the first step. You have named procrastination. Rama is naming the same swooping and dropping. It is an ordinary pattern, not a flaw in you.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: Arjuna says this, and he was the finest archer of his time. He admits his own mind won't obey him. If yours keeps replaying the same conversation at 2 a.m., you are in good company, and the Gita takes the problem seriously before it offers anything.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has just heard that a steady mind sees all beings as equal. Arjuna objects. He says his own mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He thinks it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse records this honest complaint. It proposes that the mind is difficult to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it over time. You keep telling yourself you will begin studying today, and the day slips away. This verse names that exact friction without calling you careless.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.
verse_text.translation: Let the moth fall into the blazing flame not knowing that it burns; let the fish swallow the bait not knowing the hook. But we, knowing full well, still do not let go of desires tangled in a net of dangers. Ah, how deep is the power of delusion!

reading: You feel guilty about picking up your phone again after four hours of screen time before noon. Bhartrihari says the moth does not know the flame burns, yet we know the danger and still do not let go. You already see the harm, and this verse names that shared human pull rather than judging you. Tonight, leave the phone in another room before noon.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this to the reader from his section mocking the failure to give up pleasures. He points to the moth that falls into flame without knowing it burns, and the fish that swallows bait without knowing the hook. Yet we humans see the danger clearly and still cling to desires caught in a net of harm. He asks us to let go before we are forced to, and to stop calling relief happiness. You already see the harm in those four hours before noon, and this verse names that pull as a shared human pattern rather than a personal failure.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.

reading: You notice that even after getting the last item, it already feels old. The poet observes that we know the flame burns, and yet we do not let go. That same knowing and still clinging can live in the pull toward the next car or watch.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks from his poem mocking our failure to give up pleasures. He looks at a moth and a fish. The moth flies into the flame without knowing it burns. The fish swallows the bait without seeing the hook. Bhartrihari says we are worse than both. We see the danger clearly. We know desire is tangled in a net of harm. Yet we still do not let go. He calls this the deep power of delusion. You got the last watch three months ago and it already feels old. The verse shows that knowing the next purchase will fade does not stop the pull toward it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel stuck while sale notifications control you and your closet stays full of tagged items. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go through contact with sense objects, so they do not last. You can bear this pull without letting it sweep you away, noticing the tags still on those things as a sign of what has touched you today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna reminds him that the true self is never born and never dies. Then he tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and the world brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These feelings come and go. They do not last. Arjuna must bear them patiently. The verse says that what you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain. The pull of the sale and the full closet are sensations that arrive and leave. You do not have to let them decide who you are today.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.

meaning: Bhartrihari speaks from The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures. He watches creatures act from ignorance. The moth flies into the flame without knowing it burns. The fish swallows the bait without knowing the hook waits. But humans see the danger and still clutch desires wrapped in a net of harm. The poet calls this delusion. He asks us to release what traps us before force releases us. Relief is not happiness. Your late night with reels fits this pattern. You see the cost, yet the next one still pulls you in. That restlessness is the net tightening, not a failure in you.

verse_text.speaker: Nidagha
verse_text.setting: Nidagha on craving.
verse_text.line: Every good quality I take up, craving gnaws through, like a mouse chewing a string.
verse_text.translation: Whatever good quality I take refuge in, great sage, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string.

reading: You described how the high of each purchase lasts only a day before you plan the next one. The Maha Upanishad says that whatever good quality we take up, craving gnaws through it, like a mouse chewing a string. This verse names the quiet fraying behind your flat savings, without calling it a personal failure. You might notice the next string you are trying to hold, and simply watch where the nibbling shows up.

verse_text.speaker: Indra, disguised as a jackal
verse_text.setting: The jackal tells Kashyapa that getting more will not cure his discontent.
verse_text.line: Getting what you want doesn't satisfy. Craving grows like a fire fed with more wood.
verse_text.translation: There is no satisfaction in getting what you want. Craving is not put out by water; it only blazes up more, like a fire fed with fuel.

days.reading: Bhishma, speaking through a jackal, says that getting what you want does not satisfy craving. Like a fire fed with more wood, it only blazes higher. This speaks to the restlessness you carry as a student, where each sweet glance or small win only stirs the next wanting instead of quieting it.

verse_text.speaker: Yama
verse_text.setting: Nachiketa has refused wealth and long life; Yama begins teaching.
verse_text.line: The good and the pleasant both knock. The wise choose the good; the foolish grab the pleasant.
verse_text.translation: The good and the pleasant both come to a person. The wise one examines them and tells them apart. The wise chooses the good over the pleasant; the dull chooses the pleasant, for getting and keeping.

days.reading: Yama tells Nachiketa that the good and the pleasant both come to a person, but the wise examine them and choose the good while the dull grab the pleasant for getting and keeping. You feel restless as you study, drawn to what looks sweet the moment you see it. Today, your job is simply to stand on the ground of pausing and asking whether what you reach for is good for you or just pleasant right now.

verse_text.speaker: Manki
verse_text.setting: Manki, after his last savings are lost in a freak accident, speaks to his own desire.
verse_text.line: Desire, I know your root: my own imagining. I'll stop feeding you, and you'll be gone.
verse_text.translation: Desire, I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will not imagine you any more, and you will be gone, root and all.

days.reading: Manki tells his own desire, 'I know your root: you are born of my own imagining. I will stop imagining you, and you will be gone.' You notice how a sweet look pulls you in, and you keep breaking the daily vow you make. The verse invites you to notice the picturing itself, and to stop feeding that mental fixing. When the next craving rises, rest your attention on the plain fact of the moment, not on the imagined scene.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Like a tortoise pulling in its limbs, draw your senses back from what pulls at them.
verse_text.translation: When, like a tortoise drawing in its limbs on every side, a person withdraws the senses from their objects, his wisdom is firmly set.

days.reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that a steady mind looks like a tortoise pulling in its limbs. You could try one small move today: close the tab or put the phone face-down when the pull starts. Notice the wanting fade on its own, without forcing it away.

verse_text.speaker: Vasishtha
verse_text.setting: Vasishtha teaches the disheartened young Rama that effort, not fate, shapes his life.
verse_text.line: When your mind drifts to harmful things, steer it back to good ones. That's the whole teaching.
verse_text.translation: When the mind has sunk into bad things, bring it down into good ones with effort. That is the summary of all the scriptures.

days.reading: Vasishtha tells Rama: when the mind sinks into harmful things, steer it back to good ones with effort. You could try this when you reach for something sweet again—shift your attention to one small good thing, like drinking water or stepping outside. This redirecting is the heart of the teaching, not a judgment on your wanting.

story.title: Manki's song: desire, I know your root
story.summary: Manki spends all he has on a pair of oxen; both are killed in an accident. In his despair he sees through desire: it is born of his own imagining, and he resolves to forgive insults and stop feeding it. Bhishma adds Janaka's verse on owning nothing.
story.lesson: Desire grows from what we imagine. Stop feeding it, and it fades.

days.reading: Manki puts his last money into two young bulls, and a camel runs off with them, leaving him to watch his final investment dangle and die. Out of that weariness, he turns on desire itself, saying it is born of his own imagining and will vanish if he stops feeding it. You keep swearing to stop at the sight of sweetness yet reach anyway; today, notice that the wanting lives in the imagining, and let the bulls go.

That quiet nibbling can show up in your own drive today, fraying a resolve before it holds. Notice where the wanting itself is already at work.
meaning: Nidagha speaks to Ribhu, his teacher, after returning from pilgrimage with his hopes broken. He says that whatever good quality he takes up, craving cuts it away, as a mouse gnaws through a string. The verse names a restless mind that quietly undermines every resolve before it can hold. Your own drive to always want more can quietly fray the resolve you are building right now, before it ever holds.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You order things online every week and the house fills up, yet the emptiness stays. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure means to him, and who he really is. That same question can meet you now: the things you gather do not have to define what matters, and the quiet behind them is a place to ask who you are.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You stayed up gaming till 4am on weeknights, always chasing one more match. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. Right now, your own mind may feel just as hard to steady after those late hours. You can notice this restlessness without forcing it to stop, and let the coming practice meet it where it is.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi who treats joy and pain as the same. Arjuna objects that such steadiness cannot last. The mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and he says it is as hard to hold as the wind. The Gita takes this complaint seriously and answers that practice and letting go can train it. Your late nights chasing one more match have left your mind restless and hard to steady. The verse names exactly what you are feeling without judging it.

verse_text.speaker: Vibhishan
verse_text.setting: Vibhishan, Ravana's good-hearted brother, describes his life in Ravana's court.
verse_text.line: I live here like the tongue among the teeth.
verse_text.translation: Son of the wind, hear how I live: like the poor tongue among the teeth. Friend, knowing me to be without support, will the Lord of the Sun dynasty ever show me grace?

reading: It sounds like home doesn't feel safe right now.

verse_text.speaker: Rama

reading: You have a good salary, a nice flat, and a healthy family, yet inside it all feels flat, and you ask if this is it. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasures are to him, and who he really is. meaning: Young Rama has just returned from travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he looks so low. Rama answers by questioning the worth of his future kingship and every pleasure. He asks who he is and what all this is for. He says if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your salary, your flat and your family are real, yet the inside feels flat, and you wonder if this is all there is. Rama's question meets that exact place, treating the emptiness as a doorway rather than a failure.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya
verse_text.setting: Sanjaya reports to the blind king the moment Arjuna gives up before the battle.
verse_text.line: Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed to go on.
verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: The narrator Sanjaya speaks these words. He describes the greatest archer of his time putting down his bow and sitting in the chariot, his mind sunk in sorrow. The Gita begins with someone who can't go on, and it stays with him for seventeen more chapters.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'On the Greatness of Time'.
verse_text.line: Same night, same day, the same tasks on repeat. We run in circles and call it living.
verse_text.translation: Thinking 'it is the same night again, the same day', creatures run about in vain, busy as ever with the tasks they have set going; with work full of the same repeated things, tormented by this round of existence, alas, out of delusion we feel no shame.

reading: Every day brings the same question of why you are doing all this. Bhartrihari observes that creatures run in circles through the same night and day, busy with tasks they themselves have set going, yet feel no shame. When your work has become a loop you no longer recognise, this verse simply names the repetition you are living inside today.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to the reader from his reflection on the greatness of time. He watches creatures caught in their own busyness. They tell themselves it is the same night again and the same day. They rush about with the tasks they themselves began. Their work is full of repetition. They are tormented by this round, yet out of delusion they feel no shame. The verse proposes that time slips away while we are busy repeating what we started. Your work has become a loop you no longer recognise, and the question returns because the days themselves have stopped changing. The verse names the repetition you are living inside today.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You used to love music and football, and now nothing really lands. In the Yoga Vasishtha, young Rama asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him, and who he really is. Your numbness can be the start of that same real question, not a dead end. When the next song or match comes on, let it simply be there, and notice what remains.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

reading: You feel spiritually empty, and promotions no longer stir you. Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and says again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks, and to a thinking person this feels like a mockery. That sense of being run on autopilot, with work that has lost its meaning, points to something worth noticing in your days today.
meaning: Bali, a king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and wonders what his reign adds up to. He sees the same cycle of days and nights, the same tasks rising and falling like waves. He tells himself that to a thinking person, this endless repetition feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the answer is not more work but mastering the mind that runs it. Your promotions have lost their pull because the work itself has become a loop you no longer recognise as yours. Bali's weariness points to the same thing: the mind running the same chain without a clear aim.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on how to act without being chained to results.
verse_text.line: Your work is yours to do; the results are not yours to hold. Don't let that make you stop.
verse_text.translation: Your right is to the work alone, never to its fruits. Do not let the fruit be your motive, and do not cling to doing nothing.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that your right is only to the work itself, never to its fruits. You joined a top consulting firm and each day you wait for someone to realise they made a mistake hiring you. The verse invites you to place your attention on the effort and craft you can actually control, and let the outcome rest without letting it own you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is afraid to fight because he cannot control what will happen after the battle. Krishna tells him that a person has a right only to the work itself. The results belong to something larger. The teaching is to do the work fully and let go of owning the outcome. It is not a call to stop acting. You are in a top consulting firm and you dread that the hiring was a mistake. The verse asks you to care about the work itself and to drop the grip on what the outcome will prove about you.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You are leading a team for the first time and second-guess every choice. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, as hard to hold as the wind. In that same restlessness, the Gita hears an honest confession rather than a failure, pointing toward a steadiness that practice can meet. Let your next decision rest in that recognition, not in forcing the wind still.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes the highest yogi who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last because the mind is too restless. He says the mind is turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. The verse proposes that this restlessness is real, yet practice and letting go can train it over time. Your second-guessing is not a sign that you do not belong in the role. It is the mind being restless, exactly as Arjuna named it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on being your own friend and staying steady in honour and insult.
verse_text.line: Be on your own side. Lift yourself up, don't push yourself down. You can be your own friend.
verse_text.translation: Raise yourself by your own self; do not let yourself sink. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

reading: You feel uneasy when large clients are in front of you because English does not come easily to you. Krishna tells Arjuna to raise himself by his own self and not let himself sink, since the self alone is the friend of the self. You can be the one who lifts you up in those moments, choosing to treat yourself as your own ally rather than pushing yourself down.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel you haven't earned a raise yet, so you hold back from asking. Manu speaks of finding the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitating to ask for much, not knowing its power, as doubt rises in his heart. That same hesitation can live in you today: the verse invites you to name what you want anyway, trusting the giver's generosity rather than measuring your worth by what you think you have earned.
meaning: Manu speaks to Vishnu after years of austerity. The Lord appears and tells him to ask for any boon. Manu sees that the Lord's feet fulfil every wish, yet one great longing remains in his heart. He compares himself to a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, because he does not know its power. His doubt rises in his heart, and he shrinks from naming what he truly wants. You hold back from asking for a raise because you feel you have not earned it yet. Manu shows that hesitation can come from not knowing how generous the giver really is.

Like Arjuna sitting in his chariot, you too can set down the weight of these twenty-five years and simply remain where you are for now.

He says he would rather be killed unarmed. Sanjaya then reports that Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief. Savitri tells her father-in-law that she began this vow with determination, and that same determination will carry it to the end. Your daily target already holds that same steady force, carrying you forward word by word.
meaning: Savitri speaks to Dyumatsena, her blind father-in-law and exiled king, four days before her husband Satyavan is fated to die. Dyumatsena is distressed by the harshness of her three-night vow, and she answers him calmly. She tells him she began the observance with determination, and that same determination is what will carry it to completion. The verse proposes that steady resolve is both the beginning and the force that sees a hard commitment through to its end. Your resolve to write five hundred words each day began with the same steady force, and that force can carry the work to its end without needing anything extra from you.

verse_text.speaker: Swami Vivekananda
verse_text.setting: Letter from the USA, 9 July 1895, on opposition to his work in America.
verse_text.line: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance.
verse_text.translation: Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance. Each man who thinks ahead of his time is sure to be misunderstood.

reading: You are driven by discipline and show up every day. Vivekananda writes that each work passes through ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance. If resistance meets your resolve today, you can treat it as a stage to pass through rather than a final stop. Keep going steady and true.
meaning: Swami Vivekananda writes to the Maharaja of Khetri from America in eighteen ninety five. He faces opposition from clergy there. He tells his friend that any new work moves through three stages. First comes ridicule. Then comes opposition. Finally comes acceptance. He adds that anyone ahead of their time will be misunderstood. The verse proposes that these stages are normal, not a final verdict on the work. Your daily discipline meets resistance. That resistance is a stage, not a stop sign on your path forward.

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'The Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures'.
verse_text.line: The moth doesn't know the flame burns. We know, and still we don't let go.
verse_text.translation: Let the moth fall into the blazing flame not knowing that it burns; let the fish swallow the bait not knowing the hook. But we, knowing full well, still do not let go of desires tangled in a net of dangers. Ah, how deep is the power of delusion!

reading: You have lost 15 kg and still feel the old habits calling. Bhartrihari says we know the flame burns, yet we do not let go of desires tangled in danger. You already see the risk in those old patterns, and this verse names that shared human pull without blaming you. Let that knowing sit with you today as you notice one small barrier between you and the next old habit.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks this from the Mockery of Giving Up Pleasures. He looks at the reader and points to creatures that act from simple ignorance. The moth flies into the flame and does not know it burns. The fish swallows the bait and does not know the hook waits. But humans see the danger clearly and still keep desires tangled in a net of harm. The poet calls this deep delusion. You have already lost weight and see the risk in old habits, yet they still pull at you. This verse names that pull as a shared human pattern, not a failure in you.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You promised your doctor you would walk every evening and stop the sweets, and you are holding to it. Savitri tells her worried father-in-law that she began this hard vow with determination, and that same determination will carry her to the end. Your steady resolve can do the same for you now, carrying you through each evening walk and each sweet you pass.
meaning: Savitri speaks to her blind father-in-law Dyumatsena, the exiled king. She knows her husband Satyavan will die in three days. She has begun a severe three-night vow without food. Her father-in-law is distressed by its harshness. She tells him not to grieve. She says she started this vow with determination, and that same determination is what carries it to completion. You are holding to a promise you made to your doctor. Savitri's words show that the resolve which starts a hard thing is the same resolve that finishes it.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. Your curiosity about what the Gita actually says is one of those welcome doors. You do not have to come with answers already in hand; simply opening the text with this question is enough to begin.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on a battlefield where armies stand ready to fight. He has just said that the deluded and the wrongdoers do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four kinds of good people worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search, whether trouble, curiosity, need, or wisdom, is welcome. No door is barred. Your curiosity about what the Gita actually is counts as one of those four welcome doors. You do not need to arrive with answers already formed. Simply opening the text with this question is enough to begin.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You are a second generation kid trying to reconnect with your roots, and the Gita feels like the obvious first step. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure is to him, who he is, and what all this is for. This questioning of everything he owns or does can meet your own sense that nothing matters right now, opening a real inquiry into what you are actually seeking.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels. He sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he seems so low. Rama answers with a string of questions. He asks what kingship or pleasure mean to him. He asks who he is and what all this is for. He even says if the world is unreal, let it be unreal, and asks whose it really is and what anyone has gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer. Your sense that nothing matters right now meets a voice that names the same emptiness without rushing to fix it. That questioning can sit with you as you look for what your roots might actually hold.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last. For you today, this means the anxious tightness in your chest is not a permanent state; it arises and will pass like weather. You can simply notice it without letting it sweep you away.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. Arjuna is grieving and afraid. Krishna tells him that the true self is never born and never dies. Yet the body feels heat and cold, pleasure and pain. These arise when the senses meet objects in the world. They begin and they end. They do not last. So Arjuna must bear them patiently without being carried away by either joy or grief. The anxious tightness in your chest is not a permanent state. It arises and will pass like weather. You can simply notice it without letting it sweep you away.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel your mind is overactive right now. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and holding it feels like holding the wind. This verse names that struggle plainly, showing that a turbulent mind is a real experience many face. You might notice this restlessness in a quiet moment today, and simply let the image of the wind pass through without trying to catch it.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna on the battlefield. He has just heard about a calm state where a person feels another's joy and pain as their own. Arjuna says he cannot hold to that. The mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. He says it is as hard to hold as the wind. The verse takes this complaint seriously. It says the mind is difficult to steady, but practice and letting go can train it. Your mind feels like it is racing without a brake right now. Arjuna names this exact restlessness, and the verse shows that struggling with it is the real starting point, not a failure on your part.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Rama describes his restless mind to the sages.
verse_text.line: The mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy.
verse_text.translation: The mind swoops onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later loses interest, like a child with a toy.

reading: You feel stuck and can't get started. Rama tells the sages that the mind pounces on a task like a bird on food, then drops it like a bored child's toy. This restless pattern is an ordinary feature of the mind, not a flaw in you, so when you sit down to work and the pull to begin fades, you can simply notice it as the mind letting go.

He describes what he has seen: wealth hardens people, life drips away, ego and craving drive us, the mind never fills, and time consumes everything. In the midst of this lament he offers the image of the mind swooping onto tasks like a bird onto meat, and a moment later losing interest, like a child with a toy. When work feels hollow and you cannot begin, this image names the restlessness without calling it a failure in you.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna asks what drives people to do wrong against their will; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: Why do I do the wrong thing even when I don't want to, as if something forces me?
verse_text.translation: Arjuna said: Then what drives a person to do wrong, Krishna, even against his will, as if pushed by force?

reading: You carry a weight of guilt even while raising your kids. Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong against their own will, as if pushed by force. This verse meets that honest question by naming the struggle itself as real, not as proof of who you are. When you notice that gap between what you want and what happened, let it simply be the starting point you return to today.
meaning: Arjuna asks Krishna why a person does wrong even when they do not want to, as if pushed by force. Krishna answers that unmet desire turns into anger. This desire is the enemy that clouds wisdom, and seeing it clearly is the way to master it.

verse_text.speaker: Ram
verse_text.setting: Ram has just accepted fourteen years of exile; one thing still hurts him.
verse_text.line: What hurt most was not the news, but that he didn't tell me himself.
verse_text.translation: Only one sorrow burns my heart: that the king did not tell me himself about Bharata's coronation.

reading: Your heart carries a hurt right now. Rama says the deepest sorrow is not the news itself, but that the one he loved did not face him and tell him directly. When closeness wounds you through silence or distance, naming that missing face can be the first step toward bearing what is here today.
meaning: Ram speaks to Kaikeyi after he has accepted fourteen years of exile in the forest. He agrees at once without anger. Yet one sorrow burns in him. He says only the king did not tell him himself about Bharata's coronation. The verse proposes that a person can accept a heavy loss. What wounds is the absence of a direct face to face word from the one they love. You are carrying a hurt that comes from how someone close reached you, not merely the news itself.

verse_text.speaker: Sanjaya

verse_text.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken this on the battlefield, Arjuna sank down on the seat of the chariot, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief.

reading: On the battlefield, Arjuna put down his bow and sat in the chariot, too overwhelmed by grief to go on. You feel lost right now, as if every step forward has drained away. He says he would rather die unarmed. Sanjaya then reports that Arjuna sinks down on the chariot seat, letting fall his bow and arrows, his mind overwhelmed by grief. You are in that same moment of setting everything down because the road ahead has gone dry. The verse names the freeze without calling it a final failure.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

reading: You carry a feeling of loneliness while working through your days. This invites you to notice the sacred in ordinary moments around you, so that presence stays close even when solitude feels heavy.

The verse proposes that a gentle, repeated moderation in attention settles the mind. It is not a one time achievement. verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna teaches Arjuna how to meditate and what a settled mind is like.
verse_text.line: See me in everything and everything in me, and I never lose you, nor you me.
verse_text.translation: One who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me: I am never lost to him, and he is never lost to me.

This verse does not say your loneliness is wrong. It points to a way of seeing that stays with you even when no one else is near.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You carry a peaceful feeling right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that one who is happy within, at ease within, and lit from within finds lasting freedom. That inner gladness and light can stay steady for you today, even as work goes on around you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He is describing the wise person who sees clearly. This person does not look for happiness in things that begin and end. Their delight stays inside them. Their light comes from within. Because of this, they reach the lasting peace that is Brahman while they are still alive. You feel peaceful right now. That steadiness can come from an inner source that does not depend on what happens at work or around you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on why even the fulfilled keep working for the world.
verse_text.line: Whatever a respected person does, others copy. The standard you set is the one people follow.
verse_text.translation: Whatever a great person does, others do the same. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows.

reading: You feel inspired as you run your own thing. Krishna tells Arjuna that whatever a respected person does, others copy, and the standard they set is the one people follow. In your success today, your choices quietly shape how those around you work and respond, so your own conduct becomes the quiet benchmark they take from you.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just urged Arjuna to act for the welfare of the world. Krishna now explains that people imitate their leaders. A respected person does something, and others copy it. Whatever standard that person sets, the world follows. The verse proposes that even those who have no personal need to act must keep working, because their conduct becomes the model for everyone else. Your inspiration carries weight now. The way you move through your own work quietly becomes the template others around you adopt.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna

verse_text.speaker: Bhartrihari
verse_text.setting: From 'Worship of Shiva': gratitude for a simple life.
verse_text.line: Freedom, simple food, good company, learning that brings calm: what did I do to deserve this?
verse_text.translation: This freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, living among noble people, learning whose only fruit is calm, a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long: I do not know what generous austerity this is the fruit of.

reading: You feel grateful right now. The poet wonders at a life of simple freedom, honest food, good company, and learning that brings calm, asking what generous austerity could have ripened into this. Today, you might simply notice the quiet dignity already around you—your own hours, food without humiliation, and a mind that stirs gently—and let that wonder sit with you.
meaning: Bhartrihari speaks these lines to anyone who reads his Worship of Shiva. He has just noted that moonlight, poetry and company lose their charm once the mind sees how fleeting they are. The wise leave palaces for the forest. Here he lists the goods of a simple life. He names freedom to wander at will, food eaten without humiliation, noble company, and learning whose only fruit is calm. He says a mind that stirs only gently even when it looks outward for long. He does not know what generous austerity could have ripened into this.

verse_text.speaker: Lakshman
verse_text.setting: At Lake Pampa, Lakshman pulls Ram out of despair after Sita has been taken.
verse_text.line: There is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the one who has it, nothing is out of reach.
verse_text.translation: Noble brother, enthusiasm is powerful; there is no strength greater than enthusiasm. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach.

reading: You carry a hopeful feeling as you step into this new beginning. Lakshmana tells Ram that there is no strength greater than enthusiasm, and for the one who has it, nothing is out of reach. This speaks to you today as a reminder that a small act of will can open the next chapter.
meaning: At Lake Pampa in spring, Rama sits overwhelmed by grief after Sita has been taken. Every bird and mated deer reminds him of her and his sorrow deepens. Lakshmana, his younger brother, answers this long lament by telling him that enthusiasm is powerful and there is no strength greater than it. For the person who has it, nothing in the world is out of reach. The verse proposes that resolute energy is the root of every effort and the strongest resource a person has. You are stepping into a new beginning with hope in your chest. Lakshmana's reminder can meet you here as a sign that a small act of will is enough to open what comes next.

verse_text.speaker: Savitri
verse_text.setting: Knowing her husband will die in three days, Savitri takes a hard three-night vow; her father-in-law worries.
verse_text.line: I started this with determination, and determination will carry me to the end.
verse_text.translation: Don't be distressed, father. I will see this vow through. It was begun with determination, and determination is what carries it to the end.

reading: You feel driven to keep a resolve. Savitri tells her worried father-in-law that she began this vow with determination, and the same determination will carry it to the end. Your steady resolve is what started this path and what will see it through. Let that same determination guide each step you take tonight.
meaning: Savitri speaks to Dyumatsena, her blind father-in-law and the exiled king, four days before her husband Satyavan is fated to die. Dyumatsena is distressed by the harshness of her three-night vow. Savitri tells him she began this observance with determination, and that same determination is what will carry it to completion. She is saying that steady resolve is both the start and the force that sees a hard promise through to the end. You began this resolve with clear intent. That same steady force can carry you through the nights ahead, even when the path feels steep.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: You feel curious right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that people turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom, and all four are welcome. Your curiosity places you among those who seek, and that seeking itself is counted as good. Let this openness guide the quiet mornings ahead.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just explained that the deluded do not seek him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise. He says all four worship him. The verse proposes that whatever brings a person to the search, whether trouble or need or curiosity or wisdom, is welcome. Your curiosity right now places you among those who seek, and that seeking itself is counted as good.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna on why people miss the divine and who turns to it.
verse_text.line: People turn to the divine in distress, in curiosity, in need, or in wisdom. All four are welcome.
verse_text.translation: Four kinds of good people worship me, Arjuna: the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the wise, best of the Bharatas.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of good people turn to the divine: those in distress, those seeking knowledge, those in need, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those welcome seekers. The verse simply names your open interest as a valid path toward what you are drawn to.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield. He has just said that deluded people do not turn to him. Now he names four kinds of good people who do. They are the distressed, those who seek knowledge, those who seek wealth, and the wise. He says all four kinds worship him. He does not ask them to arrive with a pure motive. He simply accepts whoever comes. Your curiosity is one of those four doors. It is already a valid way in, not a waiting room for later.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to the grieving Arjuna, on what in us is never born and never dies.
verse_text.line: Heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go. They don't last; learn to bear them.
verse_text.translation: Contact of the senses with their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. They come and go and do not last. Bear them patiently, Arjuna.

reading: You feel anxious right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that heat and cold, pleasure and pain come and go, and do not last. You can bear this discomfort like weather that begins and ends, without letting it sweep you away into panic.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna on the battlefield after Arjuna has laid down his weapons and confessed his grief. Arjuna is mourning the elders and kin he must face in battle. Krishna reminds him that the true self is never born and never dies. Then he points to the body and its senses. When sense organs meet objects, sensations arise. Cold and heat, pleasure and pain, come and go. They do not last. One must bear them with patience and not be swept away by either. Your anxiety is a sensation that has met its object and will pass, not a permanent state that defines you.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna

Notice the next wave of heat or cold as it arrives, and let it pass.

Krishna begins to teach him about the deathless Self. He says contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These arise and pass away. They do not last. One must bear them patiently. What you truly are outlasts every loss and every passing pain. In your days of caring for your parents, this points to the shifting discomforts around you as something with a beginning and an end, to be borne patiently without panic.

Your anxiety comes and goes like weather, not a fixed state. You can notice it as something that begins and ends, without letting panic carry you away.

verse_text.speaker: Bali
verse_text.setting: Bali, a king who has ruled for ages, sits by his window and wonders what it all adds up to.
verse_text.line: Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.
verse_text.translation: Again day, again night, again the same chain of tasks. Again and again: to a thinking person, I feel, this is a mockery.

meaning: Bali, a demon king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and wonders what his life amounts to. He sees the same bathing, eating and sleeping, actions rising and falling like waves, and he asks what deed would leave nothing further to do. He recalls a riddle from his father Virochana about a silent king and an all-powerful minister. The minister is the mind. Win it over through practice, and everything is won. You have built something of your own and now the days blur into the same tasks. The verse meets that blur without calling it failure.

verse_text.speaker: Manu
verse_text.setting: Manu, offered any boon after years of austerity, hesitates to ask for what he truly wants.
verse_text.line: Like a poor man before the wishing tree, we hesitate to ask for what we really want.
verse_text.translation: Like a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much, not knowing its power, so doubt rises in my heart.

reading: You feel uneasy at work, as though you are not good enough. Manu says that even before the wishing tree, he hesitates to ask for what he truly wants, not knowing its power. That doubt in your heart today might simply be not knowing how generous the giver is. You can name the wish anyway, trusting that generosity.
meaning: King Manu speaks to Lord Vishnu after years of austerity. Vishnu appears and tells Manu to ask for any boon. Manu feels that seeing the Lord's feet already fulfils every wish. Yet one great longing remains. He compares himself to a poor man who finds the wish-fulfilling tree and still hesitates to ask for much. He does not know the tree's power. So doubt rises in his heart. The verse proposes that it is not too late to turn toward what matters. But it takes courage to ask for it. You feel uneasy at work, as though you are not good enough. Manu's doubt might simply be not knowing how generous the giver is. You can name the wish anyway, trusting that generosity.

verse_text.speaker: Arjuna
verse_text.setting: Arjuna confesses the mind is as hard to hold as the wind; Krishna answers.
verse_text.line: The mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong. Holding it feels like holding the wind.
verse_text.translation: For the mind is restless, Krishna, turbulent, powerful and stubborn. I think it is as hard to hold as the wind.

reading: You feel the mind is hard to steady. Arjuna tells Krishna that the mind is restless, stormy, stubborn and strong, and holding it feels like holding the wind. In this, you are not failing; the Gita takes this struggle seriously as the honest starting point for practice.
meaning: Arjuna speaks to Krishna after Krishna describes a yogi who feels all beings' joy and pain as his own. Arjuna objects that such evenness cannot last. He says the mind is restless, turbulent, powerful and stubborn, and as hard to hold as the wind. The verse records this honest complaint. It proposes that the mind is indeed difficult to steady, yet practice and letting go can train it. Your mind races through the day's tasks and worries, and that restlessness is real. The Gita names this struggle as the honest starting point, not a sign that you are failing at calm.

verse_text.speaker: Rama
verse_text.setting: Young Rama, back from his travels, tells the sages in his father's court why nothing interests him.
verse_text.line: What is a kingdom to me, or pleasure? Who am I, and what is all this for?
verse_text.translation: What is kingship to me, and what are pleasures? Who am I, and what is all this that has come to me? If it is unreal, let it be unreal; whose is it, and what has anyone gained?

reading: You feel empty, as though nothing matters anymore. Young Rama asks what a kingdom or pleasure is to him, and who he really is amid all that has come to him. That questioning can meet you exactly where you are today: not as a flaw, but as an opening to look again at what is real.
meaning: Young Rama has just returned from his travels and sits in his father's court. Vishvamitra and Vasishtha ask why he looks so low. Rama answers with a string of questions. He asks what kingship means to him and what pleasures are worth. He asks who he really is and what all this is for. If the world is unreal, let it be unreal. He wants to know whose it is and what anyone has actually gained. The text treats this honest naming of emptiness as the first step of inquiry, not as a final answer.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna answers Arjuna's question: what does a person of steady mind look like?
verse_text.line: Dwell on something and you get attached; attachment becomes wanting, and blocked wanting turns into anger.
verse_text.translation: When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From attachment comes desire, and from desire, anger.

reading: You are feeling angry while raising kids. Krishna tells Arjuna that when someone dwells on objects, attachment is born, and from attachment comes desire, which blocked turns into anger. This points to how anger can grow from repeatedly turning something over in the mind until it feels needed. You might notice where your mind keeps returning today, and simply rest there without pushing it away.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna after Arjuna asks what a person of steady wisdom looks like in speech, posture and walk. Krishna has just warned that the senses can carry away even a wise person's mind. Now he traces the inner chain. When a person dwells on objects, attachment to them is born. From that attachment comes desire, and when that desire is blocked, anger arises. Steadiness, then, is built by guarding where attention rests. Your anger while raising your children may be growing from something you keep turning over in your mind until it feels necessary. The verse points to that habit of return rather than to the fault of anyone around you.

He treats his own emptiness as an honest question that opens the teaching, not as a flaw to fix. You are between things right now, and that emptiness is real. Rama names the same hollowness without rushing to fill it, so your feeling can simply be there.

He then tells Arjuna that contact between the senses and their objects brings cold and heat, pleasure and pain. These sensations come and go and do not last. Arjuna must learn to bear them patiently without being carried away by either joy or grief. Your anxiety right now is a sensation that arrives through contact and will also pass. It does not erase who you are beneath it.

reading: Krishna tells Arjuna that four kinds of people turn to the divine, and all are welcome: those in distress, those seeking wealth, those seeking knowledge, and the wise. Your curiosity places you among those seeking knowledge, and that alone is enough to count as good. Let this verse meet you where you are, as you sit with your books today.

reading: You feel restless. Bali says, 'Day again, night again, the same tasks again, over and over. A thinking person feels mocked by it.' This verse names the loop you are in without calling it failure. It points to the mockery a thoughtful mind senses when repetition has no end, leaving room for you to notice what your days are actually for.
meaning: Bali, a king who has ruled the three worlds for ages, sits by his window and wonders what his endless reign adds up to. He speaks to himself. He notices that day follows night and the same tasks return again and again. To a thinking person, this repetition feels like a mockery. The verse proposes that when life feels like a loop, the work is not to add more tasks but to master the mind that runs them. Your restlessness names a loop that has no end in sight. The verse points to the mind that keeps the loop turning, so you can look at what is actually driving your days.

verse_text.speaker: Krishna
verse_text.setting: Krishna to Arjuna on the inner happiness of one who sees clearly.
verse_text.line: Happy within, at ease within, lit from within: that person finds lasting freedom.
verse_text.translation: One whose happiness is within, whose delight is within, and whose light is within, that yogi becomes one with Brahman and reaches the peace of Brahman.

reading: You carry a peaceful feeling right now. Krishna tells Arjuna that the one whose happiness, delight and light are all within finds lasting freedom. That inner gladness can stay steady even as your work life shifts around you. You might notice where your calm comes from, and let that inner source simply be present today.
meaning: Krishna speaks to Arjuna while teaching the yoga of knowledge. He describes the wise person who looks with an equal eye at all beings. This person does not swing between elation and despair. Their happiness, delight and light come from within. Sense pleasures begin and end, and they lead to sorrow. The wise one sees this clearly. They withstand desire and anger. Because their joy is rooted inside, they become one with Brahman and reach the peace of Brahman while still living on earth. That steady calm you carry can rest on something deeper than the day's tasks. It does not depend on the next meeting or the next deadline.
